He put the psalmist's abandonment in the Bible. He answered "help my unbelief" with healing and not with a lecture. The God you are questioning is not fragile, and he is not offended by your honesty. He is far more grieved by the pious performance that hides the ache than by the ache itself.

You were not put here to be the emotional caretaker of everyone else's faith while your own goes unexamined and unfed. You are a thinking, questioning image-bearer of God, and your questions belong in the church, spoken out loud, taken seriously, sat with by people who will not rush to resolve them because they are afraid of them. The church that could not hold your doubt was too small. It was not your faith that failed. It was our courage.

Keep the question inside the faith rather than leaving to keep it. The doubt is not the door out. It can be the way in, because a God who is true has nothing to fear from an honest question, and the church that finally learns this will discover it was the doubters, all along, who were taking God the most seriously. They were the ones who refused to lie about him. That was never the weak faith. We only called it that because it frightened us.
excerpt: In a lot of churches the men were allowed to wrestle and the women were expected to keep the peace. But doubt is not a failure of faith. It is often faith refusing to lie.

title: The Proverbs 31 Woman They Turned Into a Checklist
body:
There is a passage of Scripture that has been used to exhaust more women than perhaps any other in the Bible, and it was never meant to. Proverbs 31, the closing poem of the book, the portrait beginning "An excellent wife who can find? She is far more precious than jewels" (Proverbs 31:10). I have watched women read it and wilt. I have watched it printed on the walls of women's ministry rooms as a standard to reach, a list of everything a godly woman is supposed to be doing all at once, and I have watched it land as an accusation. She rises while it is still night. She works with willing hands. She plants a vineyard. She makes her own clothing. She is never idle. And the woman reading it, running on four hours of sleep with a sink full of dishes, hears one thing: you are not enough, and here is thirty verses of proof.

That reading is not just discouraging. It is a mistranslation of the poem's whole purpose, and I want to show you why by going back to the Hebrew and to the shape of the text, because when you see what it actually is, it stops being a weapon and becomes what it was always meant to be, a blessing.

Eshet chayil, a woman of valor

The poem opens, in Hebrew, with the phrase eshet chayil. Our English versions render it "excellent wife" or "virtuous woman," and those translations are not wrong exactly, but they are pale. The word chayil is a warrior word. It is used throughout the Old Testament for military strength, for armies, for might, for valor in battle. When it describes Gideon, it is translated "mighty man of valor" (Judges 6:12). When it describes the men David gathered, it means warriors, men of strength. It is a word of force and courage and power.

So eshet chayil does not mean a tidy, compliant homemaker. It means a woman of valor. A mighty woman. A woman of strength and force. The same word used for warriors is used for her, and it is used deliberately. The poet is not describing a delicate domestic ideal. The poet is describing a woman with the strength of an army, and the whole poem that follows is an unfolding of what her valor looks like in the ordinary theater of a life.

The Jewish tradition understood this. In observant Jewish homes, Proverbs 31 is sung, not assigned. On Friday evening, at the beginning of the Sabbath, the husband sings this poem to his wife, aloud, as a blessing over her, a song of praise and honor for the woman she is. It is not a performance review. It is a serenade. It was never meant to be a standard she has to meet by Monday. It was meant to be a song sung over her, a naming of her strength, a public honoring of her valor. Somewhere between that Sabbath table and the American women's ministry wall, we turned a husband's love song into a manager's checklist, and we should grieve the loss of everything that transformation cost.

Notice, too, where this poem sits in the book. Proverbs is bracketed by two female figures. It opens with Lady Wisdom, personified Wisdom, a woman who calls out in the streets, who was beside God at the creation of the world, "then I was beside him, like a master workman" (Proverbs 8:30). And it closes with this woman of valor. The book that has spent thirty-one chapters commending wisdom to a young man ends by embodying that wisdom in a woman, so that the eshet chayil is not merely a good wife but a living portrait of Wisdom herself walking around in an ordinary life, buying fields and feeding her household and opening her mouth with instruction. To read her as a domestic checklist is to miss that she is the book's final and fullest picture of what a life of wisdom actually looks like. She is the answer to the whole book, and the answer wears the face of a woman.

The shape of the poem tells you it is a song

There is a structural feature of Proverbs 31 that most English readers never see, because it cannot survive translation. The poem is an acrostic. Its twenty-two verses each begin, in order, with a successive letter of the Hebrew alphabet, aleph to tav, the first letter to the last. This is a poetic form, a deliberate literary architecture, the same form used in several of the Psalms and in the book of Lamentations.

An acrostic is not a to-do list. No one writes a checklist as an alphabetic poem. The acrostic form signals completeness, an A-to-Z portrait, a way of saying this is the full picture, the whole of a life, sung in a form that is meant to be beautiful and memorable and total. The very structure of the passage tells you it is a work of praise, a poem, a song, and not a set of tasks to be audited against a woman's Tuesday. When you read it as a checklist, you are reading a wedding toast as if it were a job description, and no wonder it exhausts.

The scholar who reintroduced the valor

The writer Rachel Held Evans, in her 2012 book A Year of Biblical Womanhood, did the church a real service on this point, whatever else one makes of her broader work. She spent time learning from Jewish women who told her that in their tradition, eshet chayil is not an unreachable standard but a blessing women speak over one another. A friend finishes a hard degree, and the other women say eshet chayil, woman of valor. A mother gets through a brutal week, and her friends say eshet chayil. It is spoken as praise, as recognition, as honor, in real time, over ordinary faithfulness. It is the Hebrew equivalent of "well done, you mighty thing," said between women who see each other's strength.

That is what the phrase was for. It was a way of catching each other doing something valorous and naming it out loud. It was never a bar set impossibly high and then held over a woman's head to prove her inadequate. We took a phrase women were meant to speak over each other in celebration and turned it into a phrase men could hold against women in judgment. That is nearly the exact opposite of its purpose, and the reversal is on us.

There is one other woman in Scripture called by this exact phrase, and she is worth knowing, because she demolishes the domestic-checklist reading all by herself. In the book of Ruth, Boaz says to Ruth, "for all my fellow townsmen know that you are a worthy woman" (Ruth 3:11). The Hebrew there is eshet chayil, the very phrase from Proverbs 31, a woman of valor. And who is Ruth at that moment? She is a foreigner, a Moabite, a childless widow with no property and no security, a woman who has gleaned in the fields at the edges of other people's harvests to keep herself and her mother-in-law alive. She has not planted a vineyard. She does not run a household of servants. She owns nothing. And she is named a woman of valor because of her loyalty, her courage, her refusal to abandon Naomi, her willingness to risk everything on the kindness of a God she barely knew. The Bible attaches the phrase eshet chayil not to a woman who has completed a domestic to-do list but to a destitute immigrant whose valor was entirely a matter of character. If Ruth is a woman of valor, then the phrase was never about the checklist. It was always about the heart.

What she actually is

Now look at what the woman of valor actually does when you read her as a portrait rather than a mandate. She is not confined to a narrow sphere. "She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard" (Proverbs 31:16). She is engaged in real estate and agriculture, making economic decisions with independent judgment. "She perceives that her merchandise is profitable" (Proverbs 31:18). She runs a business; the text says she trades. "She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy" (Proverbs 31:20). She has a public ministry of mercy. "She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue" (Proverbs 31:26). She is a teacher of wisdom, torat chesed, the law of kindness, on her tongue.

This is not a shrinking domestic figure with no world beyond her doorstep. She is a businesswoman, a landowner, a manufacturer, a philanthropist, a teacher, and a mother and wife, and the poem presents all of it as one integrated life, held together without apology and without the sense that any part is in competition with another. The woman the church sometimes uses to shame ambitious women out of the public sphere is, in the actual text, a woman running enterprises and speaking wisdom in the gate. We did not just turn her into a checklist. We turned her into a smaller woman than the poem describes, and then used the shrunken version to keep women small.

The verse everyone skips

And here is the verse the checklist readers always skip, the one that dismantles the entire performance reading if you let it. Near the end, after all the labor and the valor, the poem says, "Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised" (Proverbs 31:30). The whole thing does not finally rest on her productivity at all. It rests on her fear of the LORD, her relationship with God, the reverent trust that is the beginning of wisdom in this very book (Proverbs 1:7). Everything else, the rising early, the vineyard, the trading, flows out of that one thing and is not a substitute for it. Strip away the fear of the LORD and the valor has no root. Keep the fear of the LORD and the specific tasks were never the point.

The poem is not saying, do all these things and then you will be worthy. It is saying, here is what a life rooted in the reverence of God can look like, sung in praise, and the root is the reverence, not the tally. A woman who does none of the specific things listed, who does not sew or trade or plant, but who fears the LORD, has the one thing the poem says finally matters. The checklist gets that exactly backward, making the works the foundation and the God an afterthought, which is the same reversal that turns all of grace into all of law.

The verdict

So I want to take the poem back from the way we have used it. It was a husband's Sabbath song, sung over a woman to honor her. It was a warrior word, eshet chayil, naming her strength like an army's. It was an acrostic, a complete and beautiful portrait, not a punch list. It was a picture of a woman with a full public life and a business and a ministry and a mouth full of wisdom, not a woman confined to a kitchen. And it ended by saying that none of the labor was the point, only the fear of the LORD underneath it.

We took all of that and made it a stick to beat tired women with. I have watched it done, and I have stood by while it was done, and the women who wilted under it deserved the song and got the checklist instead. If your church handed you Proverbs 31 as a standard you were failing to meet, your church handed you the poem upside down. Turn it back over. It was always meant to be sung to you, not held against you. You are the woman of valor. Someone was supposed to be telling you so this whole time. Let me be the one who finally does. Eshet chayil. You mighty thing. Well done.
excerpt: The eshet chayil is not a to-do list for exhausted women. She is a woman of valor, a warrior word, and the poem was written to be sung over women, not held against them.

title: Single Women in the Church: More Than 'Waiting'
body:
A woman in my congregation told me once that she had stopped counting the sermons on marriage. Not out of bitterness. Out of arithmetic. She was forty-one, she had never married, and she had done the math on what the church had said to her and about her over two decades of faithful attendance. The overwhelming category into which she had been sorted was not yet. She was a person defined by what had not happened.

I did not have a good answer for her that day. I have one now, and it starts with a confession. The church I serve, the church I was formed by, has a grammar of singleness that is almost entirely a grammar of absence. Single people are waiting. Single people are in a season. Single people are being prepared. Every one of those sentences locates the meaning of a person's life in a future event that may never come. We would never say it out loud in those terms. But the woman doing the arithmetic heard it clearly, because arithmetic does not lie.

The category the New Testament does not use

Here is what should stop us. The center of the Christian faith is a single man. Jesus of Nazareth never married, never fathered children, and died at roughly thirty-three. If the fullest human life is the married one with a household of children, then the most fully human person who ever lived missed it. That sentence is either blasphemy or it means our arithmetic is broken.

Paul, the man who wrote most of the New Testament, was almost certainly unmarried when he wrote his letters, and in 1 Corinthians 7 he does something the modern church has quietly buried. He commends singleness. Not as a holding pattern. As a gift. "I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one of one kind and one of another" (1 Corinthians 7:7). Read that slowly. The gift language, the Greek charisma, is the same word Paul uses for prophecy and teaching and the other manifestations of the Spirit. Singleness is not the absence of the gift of marriage. It is a gift of its own.

Then he presses further, and this is the verse we skip. "The unmarried man is anxious about the things of the Lord, how to please the Lord. But the married man is anxious about worldly things, how to please his wife, and his interests are divided" (1 Corinthians 7:32-33). Paul is not saying marriage is bad. He says it plainly a few verses later that the one who marries does well. He is saying the single person has an undivided attention that the married person, by the good and God-given fact of a spouse, does not. The single woman in my congregation was not missing something. She had something. The church had never told her what it was.

How we got the arithmetic wrong

I want to push the origin of this back further than the awkward small group, because the small group did not invent it. Barry Danylak, in his study Redeeming Singleness (2010), traces the theology carefully, and what he shows is that the ancient world had a coherent reason to treat the unmarried person as incomplete. Under the old covenant, the promise of God moved through the body. Offspring were the mechanism of the covenant. To be barren, to be childless, to die without a son, was to be cut off from the promise itself. That is why Hannah wept. That is why the daughters of Zelophehad in Numbers 27 fought for an inheritance. The stakes were not sentimental. They were covenantal.

And then something happens that the church has never fully metabolized. Isaiah, writing to exiles who felt cut off from every promise, says this: "Let not the eunuch say, 'Behold, I am a dry tree.' For thus says the Lord: 'To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant, I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters'" (Isaiah 56:3-5). The dry tree. The one whose body will never carry the promise forward. God says: you will have a name better than sons and daughters. The covenant is being pried loose from biology decades before Christ arrives to finish the work.

By the time we reach the New Testament, the mechanism has changed entirely. The promise now moves through the new birth, not through natural birth. Jesus says his mother and brothers are whoever does the will of God (Mark 3:35). The single person is no longer a dry tree. In Christ, the single woman is as fruitful as any mother in Israel, and the fruit is other believers, formed and carried and raised in the faith. We inherited the old covenant's arithmetic and kept applying it after Christ had already changed the equation. We did this. I have preached the very sermons that did it.

What the church actually does to single women

Let me be specific, because vagueness is a way of not repenting. The church does three things to single women, and it does them without malice, which is what makes them so hard to name.

First, it makes them auxiliary. The married couple is the unit; the single woman is the extra. She is invited to serve the families, to babysit, to bring a dish, to be useful around the edges of the households that constitute the real church. She is welcome. She is just not central. Rosaria Butterfield has written with unusual honesty about how her own conversion happened inside a pastor's home that practiced what she calls radically ordinary hospitality, a home where the single and the married ate at the same table as equals. That table is rarer than we admit.

Second, the church makes her a problem to be solved. The impulse to set her up, to ask when, to reassure her that God has someone, is well-meant and it is corrosive. It communicates that her current life is a waiting room. Nobody asks a married woman when she will finally do something with her life. We ask single women constantly, and we do not hear ourselves.

Third, and this is the cruelest, the church often treats the single woman's celibacy as a deprivation to be pitied rather than a discipline to be honored. In a culture drowning in the assumption that sexual expression is a human necessity, the woman living a chaste single life is doing something genuinely counter-cultural and genuinely hard, and the church that should honor it instead quietly agrees with the culture that she is missing out. We adopted the world's anthropology and then wondered why our single members felt unseen.

She was not a person on the way to becoming a real member of the church. She already was one. The church just kept scheduling its life as if she were a guest.

The undivided life

So what is the gift, concretely? I have watched it in my own congregation and I want to name it rather than theorize it.

The single women I know who have made peace with the shape of their lives, who have stopped waiting and started living, have a mobility that married people do not have. When someone in the church is dying, they can go. When a family is drowning, they can move in for a week. When the mission field calls at an inconvenient hour of life, there is no household negotiation. Paul's word was undivided, and it is not an insult to marriage to say that marriage divides your attention. It is the plain fact that a woman who has given herself to a husband and children has given herself, rightly and gloriously, and cannot also give herself elsewhere without cost. The single woman can. That is not consolation. That is vocation.

There is also a witness in it that the married cannot give. The single Christian who lives with joy is a living argument that a human being does not require romantic or sexual fulfillment to be whole. In an age that has made sexual self-expression into the very definition of authentic selfhood, that argument is not small. Stanley Hauerwas has said that singleness in the church is a sign that the church does not depend on biological reproduction to grow, because it grows by conversion and the making of disciples. The single woman is not the exception to that truth. She is its clearest embodiment.

The difference between chosen and unchosen singleness

I have to be honest about a place where much of the theology of singleness, mine included, tends to cheat. It is easy to celebrate the gift of singleness when singleness was chosen. Paul chose it. The monastics chose it. A man or woman who deliberately forgoes marriage for the sake of undivided service has embraced something, and embrace is a different experience than endurance. But a great many single women in the church did not choose it. They wanted marriage. They prayed for it. It did not come, for reasons no one can explain, and to tell such a woman that her singleness is a gift can land like a cruelty, as if her disappointment were ingratitude for a present she never asked to receive.

So I want to say the harder thing. A gift is not always something you would have chosen, and it is not less a gift for arriving unrequested. The manna in the wilderness was not what Israel wanted; they wanted the food of Egypt, and they said so bitterly (Exodus 16:3). It was still bread from heaven. Paul himself calls his thorn in the flesh a thing he begged God three times to remove, and then reports the answer: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:9). The thorn was not chosen. The grace within it was real. A single woman who longs for a marriage that has not come is not required to pretend the longing is fine. She is invited to believe that the God who did not give her the thing she asked for has not therefore given her nothing, and that the undivided life she did not choose can still become, by grace, the undivided life she offers. That is not a denial of the grief. It is what the grief can become when it is carried toward God rather than away from him.

The church fails such a woman in two opposite directions, and I have watched it fail in both. It fails her by pretending the disappointment does not exist, by rushing her past the loss to the lesson. And it fails her by treating the disappointment as the whole truth, by pitying her into a permanent posture of deprivation, agreeing with her at her lowest that her life is a lesser life. The narrow path between those failures is to grieve with her and refuse to grieve for her, to hold the loss without conceding that the loss is the last word. That is hard pastoral work, and it cannot be done from a script.

What repentance looks like

I am wary of ending on application, because clean application is the death of the actual work. But I owe the woman doing arithmetic something more than a better theology of singleness. I owe her a changed church, and change is concrete or it is nothing.

It means preaching that does not assume the pew is full of married couples with children, because it is not, and it never was. It means a life together in which single people host and lead and are followed, not merely helped. It means old married men and women who take a younger single woman seriously as a whole person and not a case pending resolution. It means, above all, that we stop treating her life as a sentence with a missing word.

It also means something harder for the married among us, myself included. It means we stop treating the single woman's presence in our homes as a favor we extend and start treating it as a gift she brings. When she is at our table, she is not being included in a real family from the outside; she is part of the family of God that our little household is only a fragment of. The church is the primary family, and the biological household is the secondary one, a truth the New Testament states so plainly that we have had to work hard to reverse it. Jesus promised that everyone who has left houses and family for his sake will receive "a hundredfold now in this time, houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children" (Mark 10:29-30). The single woman is owed that hundredfold, and we are the ones who are supposed to be it.

The single woman in my congregation is fifty now. She never married. She has buried three people from our church who had no family to sit with them at the end, and she sat with all of them. She has taught more children to read Scripture than any parent among us. If the resurrection is true, and I have staked my life on the claim that it is, then on the last day she will not be introduced as the woman who waited. She will be introduced by a name better than sons and daughters, because that is exactly what God promised the dry tree, and God does not do arithmetic the way we do.

The church owes her that name now. Not at the resurrection. Now.
excerpt: The church learned to talk about single women as a category defined by absence. Scripture, and the single Christ at the center of it, refuses that grammar.

title: Women and Work: Calling Beyond the Home Debate
body:
I came to faith as an adult, out of atheism, and one of the strange things about arriving late to the church is that you can still see its arguments from the outside before you learn to feel them from the inside. The first evangelical fight I stumbled into was the one about women and work. Should Christian women have careers? Should mothers stay home? I remember thinking, with the flat literalism of a new reader, that I could not find the debate in the Bible I was reading. I found something larger and stranger, and it did not fit either side.

Two decades later I have five sons and a working understanding of how much labor a household actually requires, and I am more convinced than ever that the standard evangelical argument about women and work is fought on a field the Scriptures never chose. Both sides have accepted a framing that would have baffled the people who wrote the book we all claim to obey.

The field nobody chose

The framing is this: there is the home, and there is work, and they are two places, and the question is which one a woman belongs in. That framing feels ancient and biblical. It is neither. It is roughly a hundred and eighty years old, and it is a product of the Industrial Revolution.

Before the factory, the home and the workplace were the same building. The household was the unit of production. A farm, a shop, a trade, a bakery, a weaving business, all of it happened where the family lived, and everyone in the family labored, including the wife, including the children, including the servants and apprentices. The Greek word for household, oikos, is the root of our word economy, and that is not a coincidence. The household was the economy. The idea that a man goes away to a place called work while a woman stays in a place called home would have been unintelligible to Abraham, to Boaz, to Priscilla, to almost everyone in Scripture.

What separated the two was the factory. When production moved out of the home and into the mill, men followed the paying labor out the door, and the home was left as a place of consumption and childrearing rather than production. Only then did a new ideology arise to explain the arrangement, what historians call the doctrine of separate spheres, the belief that the man's proper realm is the harsh public world of commerce and the woman's is the tender private world of the domestic hearth. The historian Barbara Welter named a related nineteenth-century ideal the Cult of True Womanhood in a landmark 1966 essay, and its four cardinal virtues were piety, purity, submissiveness, and domesticity. That fourth one, domesticity, is the one the church baptized. We took a Victorian economic accident and called it the created order.

What Proverbs 31 actually describes

Nothing exposes this more sharply than the passage most often preached to keep women at home. Proverbs 31. The excellent wife. If you have only heard it read at Mother's Day, you have heard it sentimentally, and you have almost certainly missed what she does with her days.

She evaluates a field and buys it (Proverbs 31:16). She plants a vineyard from her own earnings. She "perceives that her merchandise is profitable" (31:18), which means she is running a business with a margin. She makes linen garments and sells them, and delivers sashes to the merchant (31:24). She is a manufacturer with a distribution channel. "She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard." The verbs are commercial. She is trading, negotiating, producing, and profiting, and the text holds all of this up not as scandalous but as the very definition of the woman "who fears the Lord" (31:30).

The passage does not describe a woman confined to a private sphere. It describes a woman whose economic activity extends into the marketplace as a matter of course, because in the ancient world there was no wall between her household and the economy. She is praised in the gates, the place of public commerce and civic life. The chapter we cite to send women home is a chapter about a woman running an enterprise.

We turned a Victorian factory arrangement into a doctrine and then found a Hebrew businesswoman inconvenient. So we read her sentimentally, which is a polite way of not reading her at all.

The word the whole thing turns on

Underneath the work debate is a bigger idea, and if you get the bigger idea the smaller debate mostly dissolves. The idea is vocation.

Vocation comes from the Latin vocare, to call, and it was one of the recoveries of the Reformation. Before the sixteenth century, the language of calling was reserved for the clergy and the religious orders. You had a vocation if you were a priest, a monk, a nun. Everyone else just had a job, spiritually second-class labor performed while the truly called people prayed. Martin Luther detonated that in the 1520s. In his treatise on the estate of marriage and throughout his writing on the priesthood of all believers, Luther argued that the milkmaid and the magistrate and the mother have callings as holy as the monk, that God milks the cows through the milkmaid, that the humblest domestic labor done in faith is worship. The word for calling, in German Beruf, comes to mean both the divine summons and one's ordinary occupation. Those two meanings fused in the Reformation and have never fully come apart.

Now hold that recovery against the work debate, and watch what happens. If vocation is the summons of God to serve your neighbor through your labor, then the question is never whether a woman should work. All labor that serves a neighbor in faith is a calling, whether it happens over a keyboard or a cradle. The mother teaching a two-year-old to speak is doing holy work. The physician setting a broken arm is doing holy work. The single woman running an accounting firm is doing holy work. None of these is a fallback from the others. Each is a place where God is at work through a human being for the sake of other human beings.

Where the harder truth lives

I do not want to make this too clean, because clean is usually a sign that I have stopped telling the truth. There are real tensions here that the vocation framework does not dissolve, and pretending otherwise would be a kind of lie.

The first is that children are not a job you can do in your spare hours, and someone has to do it. In our house, with five sons, the sheer volume of formation required, the meals and the reading and the discipline and the presence, is not a hobby squeezed around careers. It is a vocation in the fullest Reformation sense, and it is enormous, and it usually falls disproportionately on my wife in ways that our theology of vocation honors and our economy of vocation does not pay for. To say a mother's work is holy and then to structure a household as if it were free is a contradiction I have lived and not resolved. The dignity we assign in the sermon has to show up in the division of labor at home, or the sermon is a decoration.

The second tension is that work under the fall is not pure calling. Genesis 3 promises that the ground will bring forth thorns and that labor will come with sweat (Genesis 3:17-19), and that curse falls on the woman's work as well as the man's. A great deal of what women do for pay is exhausting, underpaid, and unseen, and a theology that only celebrates work as fulfillment has not read past Genesis 3. Sometimes work is just the thorns. A robust doctrine of vocation has to hold both, the dignity of the calling and the groaning of the cursed ground, without collapsing into either the prosperity gospel of the fulfilled career or the false piety that treats all ambition as pride.

The women the New Testament put to work

If the separate-spheres ideology were the created order, the early church did not get the memo, and the evidence is embarrassing to anyone who wants to keep women out of visible labor in the kingdom. Read the sixteenth chapter of Romans, where Paul greets the people he is relying on, and count the women. He commends Phoebe, a deacon of the church at Cenchreae, and calls her a patron, the Greek prostatis, a word for a benefactor with the means to support others (Romans 16:1-2). He greets Prisca, whom he names before her husband Aquila, a couple who "risked their necks for my life" and who had earlier taken the eloquent Apollos aside and taught him the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:26). He greets Mary, who "worked hard" for the church, and Tryphaena and Tryphosa, "workers in the Lord," and Persis, "who has worked hard in the Lord" (Romans 16:6, 12). The verb for hard labor, kopiao, is the same one Paul uses for his own exhausting apostolic work.

These were not women confined to a private hearth doing invisible domestic tasks. They were financing the mission, hosting the church in their homes, teaching, traveling, and laboring in ways the church visibly depended on. Lydia, the first convert in Europe, was a dealer in purple cloth, a businesswoman running a trade in luxury goods, and the church at Philippi met in her house (Acts 16:14-15). The early Christian movement, born into a Roman world with its own rigid ideas about a woman's place, kept putting women to work in the most consequential labor there was. The Victorian doctrine that a woman's calling ends at her front door cannot survive a single reading of Romans 16.

I raise this not to settle every question about office and authority, which is a separate matter that faithful churches dispute, but to make a narrower and undeniable point. The reflex that treats a woman's work outside the home as a concession to modernity, a departure from the biblical pattern, has the history exactly backward. The biblical pattern is a church staffed and funded and advanced by women who worked hard in the Lord, and Paul knew their names and wrote them down so we would too.

The verdict the debate was hiding

So I want to end by naming what I think the home-versus-work debate was actually protecting, because it was protecting something real, and I do not want to be glib about people who felt they were defending the family.

What it was protecting was the conviction that children matter, that formation is not automatic, that a household is a garden that dies untended, and that a culture which treats childrearing as an obstacle to real life has lost its mind. That conviction is right. The church that fought for it was fighting for something worth fighting for. It just chose the wrong hill. It defended the family by defending a Victorian floor plan, and in doing so it told half the church that their labor in the marketplace was a compromise and the other half that their labor at home was invisible. Both of those messages were false, and both of them wounded women I have pastored.

I have watched women wounded by both halves of this. I have watched a gifted woman apologize for her ambition as though the drive to build something good were a character flaw peculiar to women who would not stay in their lane. And I have watched a mother, worn to nothing by the unpaid and unending labor of forming small souls, absorb the message that she had opted out of anything that counted, that the real action was happening in offices she had left. I have watched the same woman, years later, told by a different corner of the church that she had betrayed her home the moment she took a paying job to keep the lights on. She could not win, because the game was rigged from the start against the possibility that her labor, wherever it happened, was simply good. Both women were lied to. Both were doing holy work. The lie in each case was the same lie wearing opposite clothes: that there is a hierarchy of callings with a woman's true place fixed somewhere on it, and that her worth is a matter of standing in the right spot. There is no such hierarchy. There is only the summons, and the faith with which she answers it.

The truth underneath is older and harder and better. Every woman is called. The mother and the merchant, the teacher and the trader, the one raising sons and the one running a firm and the many doing both at once, are all standing in the same place, the place where God works through human hands for the sake of a neighbor. The question was never whether a woman should work. The question is the one the whole Bible asks of everyone: what has God called you to, and are you doing it in faith? That question does not sort women into spheres. It summons them. And a summons is a heavier and more honorable thing than a place to belong.
excerpt: The evangelical fight over whether women should work has argued for decades on a battlefield the Bible never chose. There is an older and larger question underneath it.

title: Female Friendship: The Relationships That Sustain You
body:
I have five sons and no daughters, and one consequence of that arithmetic is that I have spent very little of my life inside the world of women's friendships. I have watched it from the edges. I have watched my wife on the phone with a friend for two hours after a hard week and get up from the couch a different person than she sat down. I have seen a woman in my congregation held together, quite literally, by three other women in a season when nothing else was holding. And I have noticed something that took me too long to notice: the church has almost nothing to say about it.

We have shelves of books on marriage. We have ministries for mothers. We have discipleship programs and small groups. But the friendship between two women, the thing that in my observation actually carries many of them through the years the marriage books never mention, is nearly absent from our teaching. We praise the covenant relationships and leave the sustaining ones undescribed. That is a strange omission for a book that opens its account of human need not with a spouse but with the plain observation that it is not good for a person to be alone.

The friendship the Bible chose to canonize

If you want to know how seriously Scripture takes friendship, notice which one it made a whole book out of. The book of Ruth is not, at its center, a romance. The romance with Boaz is the resolution. The engine of the story is the loyalty between two women, Naomi and Ruth, a widowed mother-in-law and a foreign daughter-in-law who owed her nothing.

Ruth's speech to Naomi in the first chapter is one of the most quoted passages at weddings, which is a small irony, because it was not spoken to a husband. It was spoken by one woman to another. "Where you go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. Where you die I will die, and there will I be buried" (Ruth 1:16-17). That is covenant language. It is the language of a binding, self-giving loyalty, and Ruth aims it at a bitter old woman who has just told her to go home. The Bible looked at the relationship between two women in grief and said: this is worth a book. This is worth putting in the line of the Messiah, because Ruth becomes the great-grandmother of David and stands in the genealogy of Christ. The friendship is not a footnote to the story. It is the story.

We read Ruth's vow at weddings and forget she spoke it to a woman who had nothing to offer her. Which means we have heard the most famous words about loyalty in the Bible and missed who they were for.

What was lost when friendship became sentiment

To feel how thin our idea of friendship has become, it helps to know it was once thicker. The ancient world took friendship with a seriousness we have lost. Aristotle devoted two of the ten books of his Nicomachean Ethics to it and distinguished three kinds: friendships of utility, friendships of pleasure, and the friendship of virtue, in which two people love each other for the sake of the good and become better through the loving. That third kind, Aristotle said, was rare and slow and the closest thing to the good life a human could have.

The Christian tradition inherited this and deepened it. In the twelfth century, a Cistercian abbot named Aelred of Rievaulx wrote a whole treatise called Spiritual Friendship, arguing that friendship between believers is a place where the love of God is made concrete, that "a friend is the medicine of life," and that to move from friendship to the friendship of Christ is a natural ascent. Aelred was not talking about acquaintances. He was talking about the kind of bond in which two souls are so joined that they can bear each other's burdens and speak each other's sins and still remain.

Something happened to that idea, and I think we can date it roughly. As romantic marriage rose in the modern West to absorb all the weight of human intimacy, friendship deflated. C.S. Lewis, in The Four Loves (1960), diagnosed it precisely. Friendship, he wrote, is the least natural of the loves, the least instinctive, the least necessary to survival and reproduction, and for exactly that reason the modern world, obsessed with what is natural and necessary, cannot see it. "To the ancients, Friendship seemed the happiest and most fully human of all loves; the crown of life and the school of virtue. The modern world, in comparison, ignores it." Lewis said the modern world barely believes friendship is a real love at all. We have not disproven him.

What women's friendship carries that marriage cannot

Here I have to speak as an observer rather than an insider, and I will try to do it without pretending to know from the inside what I only know from the edge.

What I have watched, over fifteen years of pastoring, is that the friendships between women carry a specific weight that marriage is not designed to carry and often cannot. A wife cannot be her husband's only interpreter of her own experience, because he does not share it. My wife's friends understand things about her life, her body, her fears, her exhaustion, that I structurally cannot understand no matter how much I love her. When she comes home from a friend, she has been known in a register I do not have access to. That is not a threat to our marriage. It is a gift to it. A wife whose only intimacy is her husband is a wife with too much weight on one relationship, and I have seen that weight crush marriages that could have survived if the woman had not been so alone.

The friendships also do something marriages are not built to do: they witness a whole life. A husband arrives partway through the story. A friend of thirty years remembers who you were at twenty, holds the earlier selves you have half-forgotten, and can tell you when you are drifting from the person you meant to become. That kind of long witness is a form of accountability the culture has almost entirely lost, and it is one of the reasons the older women in Titus 2:3-5 are told to teach the younger. The mechanism of that teaching is not a classroom. It is friendship across the generations, the older woman who has walked the road speaking to the younger one who is on it.

The friendship that also has to be able to wound

There is a strand in Scripture on friendship that the sentimental version leaves out entirely, and it is the strand that separates real friendship from mere companionship. A real friend can hurt you on purpose, for your good, and a companion who only ever soothes is not the deeper thing. "Faithful are the wounds of a friend; profuse are the kisses of an enemy" (Proverbs 27:6). And a few verses on: "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another" (Proverbs 27:17). Iron sharpening iron is not a gentle image. It is friction, sparks, the grinding of one hard thing against another until an edge appears. The friendship that only comforts and never corrects is missing half of what the book of Proverbs thinks friendship is for.

I raise this because women's friendships, for all their depth, face a particular temptation, which is the temptation to make loyalty mean agreement. To be a good friend can quietly come to mean always taking her side, always affirming, never being the one who says the hard true thing about the man she is dating or the choice she is making or the grudge she is nursing. That is not friendship at its fullest. That is a mutual non-aggression pact dressed as intimacy. The friend who will tell you that you are wrong, who will risk the friendship to say what needs saying, is rarer and more valuable than the friend who only ever agrees, and the difference between them is the difference between iron and cotton.

The reason this matters theologically is that God himself is described as a friend who wounds. "The Lord your God is in your midst," Zephaniah says, and the same God who "will rejoice over you with gladness" is the God who disciplines those he loves (Zephaniah 3:17; Hebrews 12:6). The friendship of God is not flattery. Jesus called his disciples friends, "for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you" (John 15:15), and what he made known to them included their coming failures, their pride, their need. The model of divine friendship is a candor that costs something. A women's friendship that has grown into that kind of candor, that can bear a hard word and survive it, is a stronger and holier thing than one that has stayed comfortable. Comfort is not the goal. It is a byproduct of a bond secure enough to tell the truth.

Why the church should build for it

Let me name what I think we have gotten wrong, and let me implicate myself first, because I have designed church programs for years and I have almost never designed for this.

Our default church structures are built around the family unit and the affinity group. We gather people who are alike, young marrieds with young marrieds, moms with moms, and we call it fellowship. But the friendships that actually sustain women often cut across the categories we sort them into, and they take a kind of time and depth that a weekly small group with a curriculum does not produce. Real friendship is slow. It is inefficient. It cannot be programmed, only made room for. And the modern church, optimized for attendance and engagement, is not good at making room for slow, unproductive, deep human bonds. We are good at events. We are bad at friendship. I have run the events.

The correction is not another program, which would miss the point entirely. It is a change of imagination. It is recognizing that when a woman is drowning, the thing that most often saves her is not the pastor and not the marriage seminar but two or three friends who will not leave. It is building a church culture that honors those friendships out loud, that names them from the pulpit as a form of the love of God, that treats a woman's deep friendships not as a private matter beside her real spiritual life but as part of it.

The weight this leaves

I said I watch this from the edge, and I do. But there is one thing I have seen clearly enough to stake a claim on.

At the funerals I have officiated for women, the marriage is honored, and the children speak, and those things are right and good. But over and over, the person who cannot get through the eulogy, the one whose grief is a different kind, is the friend of forty years. The one who was there before the husband and after the children left. The one who knew. Scripture put a friendship at the head of the line of David and called it worthy of a book. The church, for all its talk of relationship, has never quite believed how much a friend can carry.

And there is a warning folded into all of this for the church that means to take friendship seriously. Friendship cannot be manufactured, but it can be starved, and the modern church has a genius for starving it. A congregation that fills every night of the week with programs, that measures its health by the busyness of its calendar, leaves no room for the slow, unscheduled, unproductive hours in which real friendship is made. Friendship grows in margin, in the leftover time, in the meal that runs long because nobody had to be anywhere. A church can crowd it out with good things and never notice the loss, because the loss does not show up on any attendance sheet. It shows up years later, in the woman who is surrounded by a busy congregation and has no one to call at midnight. The remedy is not another initiative but a strange kind of restraint, the willingness to leave a night empty so that people have time to become something to one another. A church that guards margin the way it guards its programs would be doing more for the friendships of its women than any curriculum could, and it would cost nothing but the courage to do less. That courage is rarer among pastors than it should be, and I include myself in the shortage, because an empty night on the calendar feels like a failure of ministry rather than a gift of it, and I have filled far too many of them with things that mattered less than the friendships they crowded out.

The women in your congregation who are still standing after everything are usually standing on the shoulders of a friend you have never thought to thank. It is not good for a person to be alone. God said that first, before the marriages, before the children, before any of it. We keep forgetting what he meant.
excerpt: The church has praised marriage, honored motherhood, and left the friendships between women almost entirely undescribed. Scripture takes them more seriously than we do.

title: Women and Anger: The Emotion They Weren't Allowed to Have
body:
A woman sat across from me in my office and could not say the word. She circled it for twenty minutes. She was frustrated, she said. She was hurt. She was disappointed. She was struggling. What she was, plainly, to anyone who could see her hands, was furious, and she had been taught for forty years that the fury was not permitted to her, was in fact evidence that something was spiritually wrong with her, and so she had built a vocabulary of softer words to avoid the one true one. When I finally said it for her, "It sounds like you are angry," she cried, because no one had ever given her permission to be.

I have had that conversation more times than I can count, and almost always with women. Men in my office name their anger freely, sometimes too freely, sometimes proudly. Women arrive having been trained out of the word. And I have come to believe that the church, my church, the tradition that formed me, taught women a specific and damaging lie about anger, and dressed the lie up as virtue.

The lie about meekness

The lie has a text, and the text has been abused. "Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5). Somewhere along the way, meekness got translated into the absence of strong feeling, and for women in particular it got translated into the absence of anger. The meek woman is the calm woman, the soft woman, the woman who does not raise her voice or her objection. The word became a leash.

But the Greek word behind meek, praus, does not mean the absence of strength or the absence of anger. In classical Greek it was used of a war horse that had been broken to obedience, a horse with all its power intact and now under command. Meekness is not weakness. It is strength under control, force with a bit in its mouth. The meek person is not the one with no anger. The meek person is the one whose anger is harnessed to a purpose larger than the self. To teach a woman that meekness means feeling nothing is to teach her to be broken in a different sense of the word, and the church has done exactly that.

We told women that a godly woman does not get angry, and then we handed them a Bible in which God is angry on nearly every page. The contradiction was ours. They just paid for it.

The God who is angrier than they were allowed to be

Here is the fact that should have ended the whole misteaching before it began. The God of the Bible is angry. Not occasionally, not as a lapse, but as a settled and holy response to evil. The prophets are on fire with it. Amos, in the eighth century before Christ, thunders against a people who "trample on the needy and bring the poor of the land to an end" (Amos 8:4), and the anger in the text is God's own. The wrath of God against injustice, against the exploitation of the weak, against the corruption of the strong, runs through the whole of Scripture, and it is not a flaw in his character. It is his love, refusing to be indifferent to what is destroying the people he loves.

And Jesus, the meekest man who ever lived, the one who described himself as "gentle and lowly in heart" using that very word praus (Matthew 11:29), made a whip. He walked into the temple, saw the poor being exploited by the money changers, and he "poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables" (John 2:15). The gentle and lowly one flipped furniture. His meekness did not cancel his anger. It aimed it. He was not angry at the people who slighted him. He was angry at the exploitation of the vulnerable in his Father's house. That is what harnessed anger looks like: not the absence of the fire but the fire pointed at the right target.

So when we told women that a godly woman does not get angry, we were telling them to be unlike God and unlike Christ. We were not making them more holy. We were making them less like their Lord.

What the suppression actually does

Anger that is forbidden does not disappear. It goes underground and it comes back distorted, and the distortions are the specific afflictions I see in the women who were taught this lie most thoroughly.

It comes back as depression. There is old clinical wisdom, going back to Freud and refined considerably since, that some depression is anger turned inward, rage that has no permitted outlet and so consumes the person who feels it. I am no psychoanalyst, but I have watched enough women collapse into a flat, gray exhaustion that lifted the moment they were finally allowed to name what they were furious about, and I no longer doubt that some of the depression I see in Christian women is anger that was never allowed a door.

It comes back as anxiety, the constant low hum of a person who is managing a feeling she is not allowed to have, who must monitor herself perpetually to keep the forbidden thing from showing. It comes back as passive aggression, the anger that cannot be spoken directly and so leaks out sideways in the cold silence, the withheld affection, the joke that is not a joke. And it comes back, sometimes, as a sudden and disproportionate explosion, because a pressure suppressed long enough does not stay suppressed, and the woman who has swallowed her anger for years finally erupts over something small and then hates herself for it, which confirms the original lie that her anger was the problem all along.

None of these are the fruit of holiness. They are the fruit of teaching a human being that a God-given signal is a sin. And the anger was a signal. That is the part we missed most badly.

Anger as information

Anger, at its root, is information. It is the response that fires when something we value is threatened or violated. A woman who is angry that her contribution is dismissed is registering, correctly, that she has been treated as less than she is. A woman who is angry at how her children were treated is registering, correctly, that something precious was harmed. A woman who is angry at injustice in her church or her marriage is often the only person in the room whose moral instruments are still working. To teach her to distrust the anger is to teach her to distrust the very faculty that is telling her the truth.

The wisdom of Scripture is not the elimination of anger but its right handling. "Be angry and do not sin; do not let the sun go down on your anger" (Ephesians 4:26). Read the first clause again, because we skip it. Be angry. It is an imperative, not a permission grudgingly given. Paul assumes there will be anger and there should be, and then he places two guardrails around it: do not let it become sin, do not let it fester overnight into bitterness. The instruction is not do not feel it. The instruction is feel it, aim it rightly, and do not let it own you. That is a completely different theology of anger than the one most women were handed, and it is the one that is actually in the text.

The double standard we never named

There is a further layer to this, and it is the layer that makes it a justice question and not only a psychological one. The church did not forbid anger evenly. It forbade it selectively, and the selection ran along the lines of power.

A man's anger, in most of the churches I have known, was read as strength, conviction, leadership, even righteousness. A pastor who thundered was a prophet. An elder who raised his voice in a meeting was passionate about the truth. But let a woman raise her voice with the same conviction, and the vocabulary changed instantly. She was emotional. She was difficult. She was bitter, shrill, divisive, hard to work with. The identical emotion, the identical intensity, was named as virtue in the man and as pathology in the woman. We had one word for his fire and another for hers, and the difference between the words was not the anger. It was who was allowed to have it.

This is not a modern grievance imported into the text. It is visible in the text's own defense of women whose anger was justified and dismissed. Hannah, praying in anguish so fierce that Eli the priest assumed she was drunk, was misjudged by the very spiritual authority who should have understood her (1 Samuel 1:13-14). Her intensity was read as disorder. And when she explained herself, Eli had the grace to bless her, but the reflex to pathologize the woman's strong emotion was there in the house of God three thousand years ago, and it has not left. The woman who feels deeply and shows it is still, too often, the one told to calm down by men whose own heat is celebrated.

I have to sit in the indictment here, because I have done this. I have led meetings in which a man's forceful disagreement was heard as leadership and a woman's forceful disagreement was heard as a problem to be managed, and I did not notice at the time that I was applying two different standards to the same behavior. The double standard is not usually conscious. That is precisely what makes it durable. It runs underneath the awareness of the men who practice it, which is why naming it out loud is the only way to interrupt it.

The verdict, and who it convicts

I want to be careful, because anger is genuinely dangerous, and the last thing a broken world needs is more people convinced their rage is righteous. James is right that "the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God" (James 1:20), and much of what any of us feel as righteous anger is wounded pride wearing a costume. The correction to the church's lie is not the world's celebration of anger as authenticity and empowerment, which sanctifies the fire without ever asking where it is aimed. Both errors are real. Both are dangerous.

But between the church that told women their anger was sin and the culture that tells them their anger is sacred, there is the harder and truer path of Scripture, which says the anger is neither. It is a signal to be heeded, a power to be harnessed, a fire to be aimed. It can be sin and it can be holy, and the work of a mature soul is to learn the difference, which is exactly the work the church denied women when it forbade the feeling wholesale.

The woman in my office who could not say the word left able to say it. That was not the end of her sanctification. It was the beginning of it, because you cannot sanctify a feeling you are not allowed to admit you have. We told women to be less than human in the name of being holy. The God who made a whip and overturned the tables and thundered through the prophets was never asking them for that. He was asking them for what he asks of everyone, which is harder: not to feel nothing, but to feel rightly, and to point the fire where it belongs.

And there is one more thing I owe the women I taught it to, which is a picture of where the harnessed anger goes. The prophet Nathan walked into the court of a king who had committed adultery and arranged a murder, and he told a story about a poor man's lamb until David burned with anger at the injustice, and only then did Nathan turn the anger where it belonged: "You are the man" (2 Samuel 12:7). Nathan did not tell David not to be angry. He roused the anger, and then he aimed it, at the sin, including the sin in the man feeling it. That is the whole discipline in a single scene. The women I taught to swallow their anger could have been Nathans. Some of them saw injustices in our church and in their homes that the rest of us were too comfortable to see, and their anger was the accurate instrument, and we told them to put it down. I do not know how many prophets we silenced by teaching that a godly woman feels no fire. More than none. And a silenced prophet is not a quiet blessing; it is a warning God intended for the church that the church refused to hear. When the person most disturbed by a wrong is trained to distrust her own disturbance, the wrong goes uncorrected, and everyone downstream pays for the correction that never came. We did not only wound the women. We deafened ourselves.

I taught the lie for years without knowing it was one. That is the part I cannot take back. The least I can do now is stop.
excerpt: The church taught women that meekness meant the absence of anger. It taught them a lie, and the God of Scripture is angrier than any of them were allowed to be.

title: Marriage Submission Revisited: A Woman's Perspective
body:
I have watched the word submit do real damage. Not in the abstract. In marriages I have counseled, in a woman with a bruise she explained away because she had been taught that her role was to yield, in men who quoted Ephesians 5 to end a conversation they were losing. The word has been a weapon in my presence, and I have not always known how to take it out of the striking hand without seeming to take it out of the Bible. So let me try to do that carefully, because the text deserves better than either the men who wield it or the culture that wants it deleted.

I am going to argue that the standard evangelical teaching on submission gets the passage wrong at the most basic level, not because it reads too much of the Bible but because it starts one verse too late. And I want to build the case slowly enough that a skeptic can follow it and a complementarian brother can finish it feeling understood rather than beaten, because that is the standard I am held to and it is the right one.

The verse that comes first

Open to Ephesians 5. The famous instruction to wives is verse 22: "Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord." That is where the sermons usually start. But that is not where the sentence starts. In the Greek, verse 22 does not even contain a verb. The word "submit" is not there. It is borrowed, grammatically, from the verse above it, which means you literally cannot read verse 22 without verse 21, because verse 22 has no main verb of its own. The sentence begins in verse 21, and here is what it says: "submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ" (Ephesians 5:21).

Read that again. Submitting to one another. The instruction to wives is a specific application of a general instruction that Paul has just given to every believer in the church, to submit to one another. The submission of a wife is not a unique burden laid on women. It is her particular form of a mutual submission that Christ requires of all of us, husband and wife, old and young, strong and weak. To pull verse 22 out and preach it as a standalone command to women is to sever a sentence in the middle and hand half of it to one gender. We have done this for so long that we no longer notice it is a mutilation of the grammar.

The command to wives has no verb of its own. It has to borrow the word "submit" from the verse before it, the verse about submitting to one another. You cannot obey verse 22 while ignoring verse 21. The Greek will not let you.

The word that was never about a boss

Now to the harder word, the one the whole debate turns on, and I have to slow down here because this is where careful scholarship matters and where sloppy scholarship has done the most harm. Paul tells husbands, in verse 23, that the husband is the "head" of the wife as Christ is the head of the church. The Greek word is kephale, and the entire question is what it means.

The assumption in most evangelical preaching is that head means boss, authority, the one who commands. And in modern English, head does mean that. The head of a company gives orders. But Greek is not English, and the word carried a range of meanings, and there is a genuine, unresolved scholarly debate about which one Paul intends. Some scholars, following the work of Wayne Grudem, argue that kephale in Greek regularly meant authority over. Others, following Gordon Fee, Philip Payne, and the earlier work of Catherine Kroeger, argue that kephale more often meant source or origin, as we still speak of the head of a river, the headwaters, the place a thing flows from. I am not going to pretend this debate is settled, because it is not, and any preacher who tells you it is settled is selling you his side as if it were the text.

But watch what Paul does with the word, because his own usage is the best commentary on his meaning. Having called the husband the head, he does not then tell the husband to command. He tells him to die. "Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her" (Ephesians 5:25). The model of headship Paul offers is the cross. Christ's headship over the church is expressed not in issuing orders but in laying down his life. Whatever kephale means, Paul defines it by Calvary, and Calvary is the opposite of the domineering authority the word has been used to justify. If the husband is the head as Christ is the head, then the husband's headship is measured by his willingness to be crucified for his wife, not by his power to overrule her.

The three verses given to wives are about submission. The nine verses given to husbands are about a love that costs the husband everything, up to and including his life. If Paul wanted to establish male authority, he built a strange case, because he gave the man the far heavier command and defined it by death.

The revolution hidden in a household code

To feel how radical this passage was, you have to know what it was responding to, and here the history is not decoration, it is the whole point.

The literary form Paul is using was well known in the ancient world. Scholars call it a household code, a set of instructions for the ordering of a household, and there were pagan versions of it going back to Aristotle's Politics, which laid out the relations of husband to wife, father to child, master to slave. Every ancient reader knew the form. And in every pagan version of the form, the instructions ran in only one direction. The wife was told her duties to the husband. The child was told its duties to the father. The slave was told its duties to the master. The powerful party was not addressed at all, because the powerful party had no duties. Power was the freedom from obligation.

Paul takes this form and does something that would have startled his first readers. He addresses the powerful. He turns and speaks directly to the husband, to the father, to the master, and lays obligations on them. He tells husbands to love with the self-giving love of Christ. He tells fathers not to provoke their children (Ephesians 6:4). He tells masters to stop threatening and reminds them they have a Master in heaven who shows no partiality (Ephesians 6:9). In a world where power meant the absence of duty, Paul told the powerful they had duties, and grounded those duties in the God before whom the master and the slave stand equal. That is not a defense of the ancient hierarchy. It is the beginning of its unraveling, a bomb planted inside the household code with a slow fuse.

Where I land, and what I have not answered

The Constitution I write under requires that I name where I stand, the tradition it comes from, and the strongest objection I have not fully answered. I will do that, because a steelman that hides the author's own position is a dodge.

I land closer to what is usually called the mutualist or egalitarian reading, though I am not comfortable with the tribal shape those labels have taken. I believe verse 21 governs the whole passage, that mutual submission is the frame and not a preface to be discarded, that Paul's definition of headship by the cross empties the word of the domineering meaning it has been given, and that the trajectory of the passage runs toward the dignity and near-equality of the wife rather than away from it. This is a second-order question. Faithful churches divide over it, and the creeds do not bind it. A godly complementarian and a godly egalitarian are brother and sister, and I refuse to make this the wall of the faith when Scripture makes it something less.

And here is the objection I have not fully answered, stated in the form my complementarian brothers would recognize as fair. Even granting mutual submission in verse 21, Paul still gives the wife and the husband different applications of it. He does not tell husbands to submit to wives in verses 22 through 24; he tells wives to submit and husbands to love as head. The differentiation is in the text, and a reading that flattens it entirely has to explain why Paul bothered to address the two differently at all. That is a real argument. I find the cross-shaped definition of headship answers most of its force, but not all, and I would be lying to say the differentiation vanishes. It does not. I hold my position with conviction and without contempt for the brother who reads the same verses and lands a step to my right.

What submission is not, in the woman's own account

I promised a woman's perspective, and though I am a man writing it, I have listened to enough women wrestle honestly with this text to report what the faithful ones actually conclude, as against both the caricature the world paints and the distortion the abuser imposes. The women I know who submit to this passage with joy rather than fear describe something the popular debate never captures, and it is worth putting in their terms.

They say, first, that submission in Ephesians 5 is not obedience. Paul had a perfectly good word for obedience, hypakouo, and he uses it a chapter later when he tells children to obey their parents and servants to obey their masters (Ephesians 6:1, 5). He does not use it for wives. He uses hypotasso, to place oneself in order under, a word with a voluntary and self-giving quality that the word for obedience lacks. A wife is never told to obey her husband in this passage. She is invited to a freely chosen yielding, which is a categorically different thing than the commanded obedience of a child or a slave, and the difference is not a technicality. A woman who is commanded is a subordinate. A woman who freely places herself is a partner performing an act of love, and an act of love that is coerced is not love at all.

They say, second, that the submission is bounded by the object of ultimate loyalty. "Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord" (Ephesians 5:22). The phrase "as to the Lord" is not a way of making the husband a stand-in for God. It is the opposite. It subordinates the whole arrangement to a prior and higher allegiance. A wife submits to her husband within her submission to the Lord, which means the moment a husband asks her to sin, to violate her conscience, to betray Christ, the ordering collapses, because her deepest submission was never to him. Peter and John set the principle for every Christian when they said, "We must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29), and no marriage text overrides it. A submission that has no such limit is not the Christian kind. It is idolatry with a ring on.

They say, third, that they have never once found this text a burden when it was matched by a husband living out verses 25 through 33. The whole thing works, they tell me, or fails, on whether the man is dying. A wife's yielding to a husband who is laying down his life for her, studying her, honoring her, nourishing her as his own body, is not a hardship; it is the natural response to being loved that thoroughly. The passage was never meant to be read one clause at a time by parties looking to extract their advantage. It was meant to describe a mutual self-donation in which each gives the other more than the other could demand. The tragedy is not the text. The tragedy is every marriage in which one half of it was obeyed and the other half was not.

The verdict

Here is what I will not soften, because a woman who has been hit with this text deserves at least this much clarity.

Whatever submission means in Ephesians 5, it cannot mean what the abuser needs it to mean. A husband who uses this passage to demand, to control, to dominate, to silence, or to strike has not read past verse 22, and he has certainly not read verse 25. He has taken a text about a love that goes to the cross and turned it into a warrant for a power the text explicitly forbids him. He is not obeying the passage. He is inverting it. The very verses he quotes to justify his authority are the verses that condemn him, because they command him to a crucified love and he has chosen a crown instead.

To the woman who circled that word in fear, I want to say the thing the church too often did not: the God who wrote that passage is not on the side of the man crushing you with it. The passage begins with mutual submission and defines the husband's role by a Savior who let himself be killed rather than lift a hand against his bride. If your marriage looks like the opposite of Calvary, the problem is not that you have submitted too little. The problem is that no one has loved you the way the passage demands, and the text you have been beaten with is the very text that was meant to protect you.

We handed men half a sentence and called it the will of God. The other half is still there, on the page, in the Greek, waiting for a church honest enough to read it out loud.
excerpt: The most weaponized verse in evangelical marriage teaching begins with a sentence almost nobody reads first. Ephesians 5:21 changes everything that follows it.

title: Women and Mental Health: The Weight Nobody Sees
body:
Before I say anything else, I want to say the plain and necessary thing. What follows is a pastor thinking theologically about suffering. It is not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for a doctor, a therapist, or, if you are in danger tonight, the crisis line that exists precisely so that you do not have to be alone with the worst hour. If you are thinking of harming yourself, please reach out to a professional or call or text 988 in the United States. Theology and medicine are not rivals here. You need both, and this essay is only one of them.

Now the harder thing, the thing the church has too often gotten wrong, and that I have gotten wrong in rooms where a woman was quietly falling apart in front of me and I reached for a verse instead of a hand.

The suffering that gets a suspicion instead of a hand

A woman came to me years ago and told me she thought she was losing her mind. She could not stop crying. She could not feel her children the way she used to. She woke at three in the morning with a dread she could not name. And she said, with a shame that has stayed with me, that she was afraid to tell anyone at church, because she knew what they would say. They would say she needed to trust God more. They would find the sin. They would hand her a verse about anxiety and joy and treat her collapse as a spiritual failure she could repent her way out of.

She was not wrong about what the church would say, because it is what the church often does say, and it is a specific cruelty. We meet a suffering we cannot see with a suspicion we should never have. When a woman breaks her arm, we do not ask what sin caused it. When a woman's mind is breaking, we too often do, and we dress the interrogation up as spiritual concern. I have watched women who were clinically ill be told they had a joy problem, a faith problem, a gratitude problem, when what they had was an illness, and the church made the illness lonelier than it already was.

We would never tell a woman with a broken arm that she needed to trust God more. We say it constantly to the woman whose mind is broken, and we call the cruelty discernment.

The Bible is more honest than the sermons

What makes this failure so galling is that the Bible itself is far more honest about the darkness than the people who quote it. The suspicion the church casts on the suffering woman cannot survive an actual reading of Scripture, because Scripture is full of the faithful in the pit.

Read the Psalms and count the ones that end in darkness. Psalm 88, the darkest of them all, ends without resolution: "You have caused my beloved and my friend to shun me; my companions have become darkness" (Psalm 88:18). That is the last verse. There is no upturn, no doxology, no light breaking. The Spirit of God inspired a prayer that ends in the dark and put it in the church's hymnbook, which means that a believer sitting in unrelieved darkness is not outside the faith. She is inside a psalm.

Elijah, days after the greatest victory of his ministry, collapses under a broom tree and asks God to let him die: "It is enough; now, O Lord, take away my life" (1 Kings 19:4). This is not a man in unbelief. This is the prophet who called down fire, and he is suicidal from exhaustion. And notice what God does not do. God does not rebuke him. God does not diagnose a sin. God lets him sleep, and sends an angel to feed him, and lets him sleep again, and feeds him again (1 Kings 19:5-7). The divine response to a servant's collapse is rest and food before it is a single word of theology. God treated the body first. The church that skips straight to the sermon is less patient with the broken than God was.

And there is a phrase in the New Testament we rush past. In Gethsemane, Jesus himself says, "My soul is very sorrowful, even to death" (Matthew 26:38).
