The Son of God, in his humanity, knew a sorrow that pressed to the edge of what a soul can bear. If sorrow to the point of death were evidence of faithlessness, it would convict our Lord. It does not. It sanctifies the darkness. It means the God we worship has been in the pit and did not consider it beneath his dignity to feel it.

The weight that is specifically hers

There is a further honesty owed here, which is that women carry weights that men structurally do not, and the church has been slow to reckon with them.

There is the biological weight. The hormonal upheavals of the female body, in the postpartum months, in the long grind of the reproductive years, in the changes of midlife, are real physiological events with real effects on the mind, and treating them as moral events is a category error that harms women. Postpartum depression is not a failure of maternal love. It is an illness with a physical mechanism, and a woman drowning in it needs a physician and a community, not a lecture on gratitude for the child she is too ill to enjoy. When we spiritualize what is biological, we heap shame on a woman who is already suffering, and shame is fuel to the fire we are pretending to put out.

There is the weight of the unseen labor, the invisible cognitive load of running a household, the mental ledger of everyone's needs that so often falls to women and is never counted as work because it produces nothing you can point to. A woman can be exhausted to the bone by a labor that leaves no visible product, and be told she did nothing all day, and begin to believe it. That is a specific erosion, and it wears on the mind in ways the culture and the church have only recently begun to name.

And there is the weight of being the one who holds everyone else together. In many families it is the woman who monitors the emotional temperature of the whole household, who absorbs the moods, who manages the peace. That role is real work and it is depleting, and the person doing it is often the last one anyone thinks to check on, because her whole function is to be the one who is fine so that everyone else can fall apart on her. When she finally cannot hold it anymore, the system that depended on her holding it has no idea what to do.

What the church owes and has often withheld

So what should we have done, and what should we do now? I want to be concrete without pretending there is a four-step fix, because there is not, and anyone who offers you one for the suffering mind is selling something.

We owe the suffering woman the same thing God gave Elijah under the broom tree: rest, food, presence, and time before a single word of correction. We owe her the refusal to diagnose her illness as sin. We owe her a theology robust enough to hold Psalm 88, a faith that does not require her to fake the doxology she cannot feel. We owe her the full use of God's common grace, which includes the physician and the counselor and the medication that, for many, is not a failure of faith but a mercy of God delivered through the ordinary means of medicine, the same way an antibiotic is. The God who made the body made the ways the body is healed, and there is no more shame in a prescription for the mind than in one for the blood.

And we owe her the truth that her worth does not rise and fall with her ability to function. This is the deepest thing, and it is where the gospel actually bites. A woman whose whole life has been justified by what she produces, the clean house, the fed family, the held-together everyone, will experience her collapse as the collapse of her worth, because her worth was built on her output. The gospel says her worth was never her output. She is loved by God for reasons that have nothing to do with whether she got out of bed today, purchased at the cross, secured before she did anything and safe even now when she can do nothing. On her worst day, flattened and useless by every measure the world uses, she is worth exactly what she was worth on her best, because the price was set by Christ and not by her. That is not a verse to hand her and walk away. It is a truth to sit inside with her, for as long as it takes, in the dark, the way God sat with Elijah and the way Christ sweated in the garden.

Where the culture gets it half right

I want to test the secular account at its strongest, because the church's instinct to dismiss it wholesale is part of what made us useless to suffering women in the first place. The wider culture now speaks openly about mental health, has torn down some of the stigma, and has insisted that depression and anxiety are real conditions and not moral failures. On all of that, the culture is right, and it is right against a church that was often wrong, and honesty requires me to say so plainly.

The research the culture draws on is not fluff. The World Health Organization has documented for years that women are diagnosed with depression at roughly twice the rate of men, a disparity that holds across cultures and cannot be explained away as mere reporting bias. Whatever the tangled causes, biological, social, and circumstantial, the weight really does fall harder on women, and a church that will not say so is refusing to see what is in front of it. The secular world saw it first, named it, and stopped shaming the sufferer, and every one of those was a mercy the church should have offered and did not.

But the secular account, strong as it is on the symptom, tends to be thin on the anthropology, and this is where Scripture goes deeper rather than merely disagreeing. The culture can tell a woman her depression is not her fault. It struggles to tell her why she matters when she cannot function, because it has largely located human worth in autonomy, productivity, and self-actualization, the very things depression strips away. A therapeutic culture that grounds a person's value in her flourishing has nothing to say to the person who cannot flourish, and so it can remove the shame of the illness without answering the deeper terror underneath it, which is the fear that a self that produces nothing is a self worth nothing. Only a gospel that grounds worth outside the self, in the love and the purchase of God, can reach that terror. The culture got the symptom right and the anthropology incomplete. The church should have offered both and for too long offered neither.

The weight this leaves

The woman who came to me afraid to tell anyone got help, real help, medical and communal and slow. She is well now, mostly, in the way that people who have been to the bottom are well, which is to say she carries the memory of it and it has made her gentler with everyone else who goes there. But I think often of the fear she named, the certainty that the church would find the sin. She was not paranoid. She had watched us do it to others. We had trained her to expect a suspicion in the place where she should have found a shelter.

I think often, too, about how much of what I mistook for a spiritual condition was simply a body that had run out of what it needed to keep going. The line between the soul and the body is far thinner than my early theology allowed. When Elijah wanted to die, God did not begin with his theology; God began with sleep and bread, because sometimes the most spiritual thing a crushed person needs is rest and food and a doctor, and the reordering of the heart comes after the body has been given a chance to recover. A pastor who cannot tell the difference between a sin to be confessed and an illness to be treated will wound the very people he most wants to help, and I have been that pastor, reaching for repentance where I should have reached for a physician's number and a warm meal and a promise to stay.

That is the failure I cannot argue my way around. The Bible we hold gives us Psalm 88 and Elijah under the tree and Christ in Gethsemane, a whole scriptural vocabulary for the faithful in the dark, and we set it aside to interrogate the suffering. The weight nobody sees is heavy enough. The church was never supposed to add to it. Too often it has, and I among them. The verse I should have led with, every time, was not the one about anxiety. It was the one that says he is near to the brokenhearted, and saves the crushed in spirit (Psalm 34:18). Near. Not diagnosing from across the room. Near.
excerpt: The church has too often met a woman's suffering with a Bible verse and a suspicion. Scripture itself is more honest about the darkness than the sermons that quote it.

title: Raising Daughters in a World That Objectifies Them
body:
I have five sons and no daughters. I want to say that at the top, because it would be a kind of dishonesty to write about raising daughters as if I had done it. I have not. What I have done is pastor the fathers and mothers of daughters for fifteen years, watch the girls in my congregation grow up inside a machine that means them harm, and raise five boys who are, whether I like it or not, part of the world those girls have to survive. So I write this from beside the problem rather than inside it, and I write it partly as a confession, because the sons I am raising are being formed by the same machine, on the other side of it, to consume what it teaches them to see.

The machine has a name, or several. The academic term is the sexual objectification of women, and the developmental research on it is now substantial enough that I do not have to speculate. The girls in your house are being trained, from an age earlier than you think, to experience themselves as things to be looked at. That is the war. And the church has too often responded to it with a counter-lie that is only the same lie in a longer skirt.

The name for what is happening to her

In 1997, two psychologists, Barbara Fredrickson and Tomi-Ann Roberts, published a paper in the journal Psychology of Women Quarterly that named the mechanism with unusual precision. They called it objectification theory, and its central claim is this: when a culture persistently treats girls and women as bodies to be evaluated by others, the girls internalize the outside gaze. They begin to watch themselves from the outside. They stop asking what does my body feel and start asking what does my body look like to someone watching. Fredrickson and Roberts called this self-objectification, and their research, replicated many times since, linked it to a cluster of afflictions that fall disproportionately on girls: anxiety, depression, disordered eating, and a diminished ability to be present in one's own life because part of the mind is always occupied monitoring one's appearance.

Sit with the horror of that for a moment. A girl learns to spend a permanent fraction of her attention watching herself be watched. She is never fully inside her own experience, because a portion of her is always outside it, checking the picture. And the machine that trains her, the advertising, the algorithms, the pornographic wallpaper of the culture, the filtered images that even her friends are posting, does this to her before she is old enough to name it or resist it. This is not a moral panic. It is measured, published, and replicated developmental psychology, and it describes a genuine assault on the interior life of the girls we are raising.

She is taught to watch herself being watched, until a part of her is always standing outside her own life, checking the picture. That is not vanity. It is an injury, and it is being inflicted on purpose.

The church's counter-lie

Here is where I have to turn on my own house, because the church saw this assault and often responded with something that was not the gospel but its counterfeit. It responded with the purity culture of the 1990s and 2000s, and I watched that culture form a generation of girls, and I have since counseled the women it wounded.

The counter-lie went like this. The world says your body is a thing to be looked at and consumed. The church replied: yes, your body is a thing to be looked at, and therefore you must cover it, guard it, and manage it, because it is a stumbling block, a temptation, a danger to the boys around you. Do you hear what happened? The church accepted the world's basic premise, that the girl's value and meaning are located in her body as an object of the male gaze, and then simply reversed the instruction. The world said display it; the church said hide it. But both agreed on the thing that mattered: she is, first and fundamentally, a body that men will look at, and her spiritual task is to manage that looking.

The fruit of this was bitter, and I have tasted it in my office. Women raised in purity culture who could not experience their own bodies as good even inside a marriage the church itself had blessed, because they had been trained to see their bodies as landmines. Women who carried shame for having been looked at, as if the looking were their sin. Women who had been told, in youth group, that their bodies were the reason a boy might fall, which placed on a fourteen-year-old girl the responsibility for the imagination of every boy who saw her. That is a monstrous burden, and it is the same objectification the world practices, baptized and handed back to her as holiness. We did not free her from the gaze. We just added God's name to it.

What Scripture actually says about the daughter's body

The recovery is not a better modesty policy. It is a different anthropology, and it is right there in the text we claimed to be defending.

The first thing Scripture says about the human body, male and female, is that it was made in the image of God. "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them" (Genesis 1:27). The daughter's body is not first an object of anyone's gaze. It is first an image of God, a bearer of divine likeness, made to be a subject who looks out at the world and acts within it, not primarily an object that is looked at. Every regime that reduces her to a thing to be evaluated, whether it hands her a bikini or a burden of blame, is denying Genesis 1:27, and the church that adopted the world's premise denied it too.

And Scripture is relentless that the value of a person is not in the surface the world evaluates. "Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain, but a woman who fears the Lord is to be praised" (Proverbs 31:30). Peter writes to women that their true adornment is not the external, the braided hair and the gold, but "the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God's sight is very precious" (1 Peter 3:3-4). Read that phrase carefully, because purity culture abused it too: in God's sight. The verse relocates the audience. The girl trained by the machine performs for the gaze of the watching world. Peter tells her the audience that matters is God, who sees the hidden person and not the surface, and who has already declared her precious before she managed a single thing about her appearance. That is not another instruction about how to be looked at. It is an escape from the whole economy of being looked at.

What I am trying to do with my sons

I said this was a confession, and here is the confessing part. The war on daughters cannot be won on the daughters' side alone, because half the machine runs through boys, and I am raising five of them. The girls in your congregation will grow up into a world staffed by men, and some of those men will be mine, and the question of whether they consume women as objects or honor them as image-bearers is being decided right now, in my house, on my watch.

So the work I actually control is not the daughters' modesty. It is my sons' vision. I am trying, imperfectly and against the same machine, to raise boys who see a woman as a whole person before they see her as a body, who are not trained by a decade of pornographic saturation to evaluate before they encounter, who understand that the gaze the world taught them is not neutral looking but a habit of consumption that damages the person consumed and hollows out the one consuming. When Jesus said that a man who looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery in his heart (Matthew 5:28), he located the sin where it belongs, in the one doing the looking, not the one being looked at. Purity culture inverted that verse and hung it on the girls. I am trying to hang it back where Christ put it, on the boys, on my boys, where the responsibility actually lives.

What a father is actually for

I came to faith from atheism, and I was raised without a father, and those two facts collide most sharply for me right here, because I am now the thing I never had, to sons who will help decide how a generation of daughters is treated. A girl raised with a father who delighted in her mind before her appearance, who was interested in what she thought and not merely how she looked, who was safe and present and did not leave, has been handed a set of instruments for detecting the counterfeit long before the counterfeit arrives. She has felt what it is to be loved as a person by a man, and so the man who wants to love her only as a body has a harder time convincing her that consumption is the same as care. She has a reference point. The absence of that reference point is one of the machine's quietest advantages, and I know it from the inside, because I grew up without the male love that would have taught me what love from a man was supposed to feel like.

The research bears this out with unusual consistency, and I state it carefully because the topic is prone to overreach. Studies of paternal involvement, including the work summarized by researchers like Ronald Rohner on the effects of father acceptance and rejection, have found across cultures that a father's warm, engaged presence correlates with better outcomes for daughters in self-image, in the timing and health of their relationships, and in their resistance to exploitation. This is not a promise, and it is not a mechanism a father can operate like a lever, because children are not machines and God is sovereign over ends no parent controls. But it points at something true and old: that the way a girl is treated by the first man who loves her shapes what she will tolerate from the men who come after. The father is a witness. His love is testimony, admitted into evidence long before she can weigh it, about whether a woman is a subject to be known or an object to be used.

God knew this about himself before any of us knew it about our fathers. The name he most insists on, over against every distortion, is Father, and the psalm calls him "Father of the fatherless and protector of widows" precisely at the point where the human father has failed or vanished (Psalm 68:5). I take that verse personally, because I was one of the fatherless it names, and I have staked my life on the claim that the God it describes is real. A daughter whose earthly father fails her, or dies, or was never there, is not therefore doomed, because there is a Father who does not leave, and the church that mediates his love to the fatherless girl is doing the most direct possible work against the machine. But where a human father is present, he is not off the hook. He is on the front line, and most of us do not treat the assignment with the seriousness the girls deserve.

The weight this leaves

I cannot tell you how to raise your daughter, because I have never raised one, and I distrust the men who write confidently about a war they have only watched. But I can tell you what I have seen from beside it, and I can tell you the one thing I would stake everything on.

Your daughter is being told, by a machine of enormous power and no conscience, that she is a surface. The world says the surface should be displayed. Some of the church said the surface should be hidden. Both were lying to her about the most basic fact of her existence, which is that she is not a surface at all. She is an image of God, a subject with a soul and a will and a mind, made to look out at the world and love it and act in it, precious in God's sight before and beneath and entirely apart from whether anyone ever finds her beautiful. If she believes that, all the way down, the machine loses its grip, because the machine only works on a girl who has agreed to be a surface. And if she does not believe it, no modesty policy in the world will save her, because she will only be a well-covered object instead of an exposed one, still watching herself be watched.

The war for your daughter is not, finally, a war over her clothing. It is a war over whether she is a person or a thing. The world has picked its side. Too often the church, meaning to fight the world, picked the same side in different words. I have five sons and no daughters, and the most useful thing I can do in this war is make sure the men I am sending into it have learned to see a person where the machine trained them to see a thing. That is my part. The daughters are worth every hour of it, and I am not certain we have given them the hours they deserve.
excerpt: I have five sons and no daughters, which means I write this as an outsider to the specific war being waged on the girls in your house. But I have watched the war, and I know the lie at the center of it.

title: Doubt After Losing Someone You Love
body:
I have stood at more gravesides than I can count now, and I have learned that the doubt which comes after death is not the doubt of the debate stage. It does not arrive with arguments. It arrives with silence. You bury the person, and then you keep waking up, and the God who was supposed to be near the brokenhearted seems to have stepped out of the room at the exact moment you needed Him to stay. That is the wound. Not the syllogism. The absence.

Let me say the honest thing first, because you have been handed too much dishonesty already. The comfort you were given at the funeral probably made it worse. Someone told you they are in a better place. Someone told you God needed another angel. Someone told you everything happens for a reason and then could not tell you the reason. These are not lies people tell out of cruelty. They are lies people tell out of fear, because they cannot bear the silence either, so they fill it with noise. And you, standing there with the actual weight of the loss in your hands, knew the noise was hollow. That knowing is not a failure of faith. It may be the most honest thing you have done in months.

The Bible does not scold the griever

Here is what surprised me when I came to faith from the outside, having spent years as an atheist who assumed the Bible was a book of relentless cheerfulness. The Bible does not scold the griever. It hands the griever a microphone. A full third of the Psalms are laments, and they are not polite. The psalmist says, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning?" (Psalm 22:1). That is not a heretic speaking. That is the prayer book of Israel, and it is the prayer Jesus Himself quoted from the cross (Matthew 27:46). The Son of God died with a question of abandonment on His lips. If your grief has driven you to ask where God went, you are not standing outside the faith. You are standing inside its oldest room.

The philosopher Nicholas Wolterstorff lost his twenty-five-year-old son Eric to a mountaineering accident in 1983, and he wrote a small book afterward called Lament for a Son. He refused to resolve it. He wrote, "I shall look at the world through tears. Perhaps I shall see things that dry-eyed I could not see." He was a serious philosopher, a man who had spent his life on the strongest arguments for and against God, and when his boy died the arguments did not carry him. What carried him was permission to weep in the presence of God without pretending the weeping was faithlessness. That is the first thing I want to give you. Permission.

You do not have to defend God to grieve honestly. He is not so fragile that your tears will topple Him.

I remember the first funeral I preached after coming to faith. I stood over a casket and realized that everything I had spent my atheist years mocking, the hope of resurrection, the promise that death was not final, was now the only thing I had to offer a room full of people who could not breathe. And I was terrified, because I knew that if it was not true, I was the cruelest man in the building, selling comfort to the desperate. That terror never fully left me, and I have come to believe it should not. A faith that has never stood at a real graveside and felt the full weight of the question does not yet know what it believes. Your doubt is the graveside doing its work. It is faith being forced to say whether it means what it claimed when the stakes were low.

What the doubt is actually saying

When you sit with a doubting griever long enough, the doubt usually resolves into one of two sentences. The first is: if God is good and God is powerful, why did He let this happen. The second, quieter and more devastating, is: if I cannot feel Him now, was He ever there at all. These are different wounds and they need different care, so let me take them one at a time.

The first is the old problem of suffering, and I will not insult you by pretending there is a clean answer that makes the pain evaporate. There is not. The philosopher Alvin Plantinga did real work here in the 1970s, showing that there is no logical contradiction between an all-good, all-powerful God and the existence of evil, because it is possible that God permits suffering for reasons we cannot see. That argument holds. But notice what it does and does not do. It shows that your grief is not proof God does not exist. It does not show you the reason. It clears the ground; it does not fill the grave. A person who has just lost their child does not need a proof that God could have reasons. They need to know they are allowed to not know the reason and keep believing anyway. The book of Job spends thirty-eight chapters building toward the reason, and when God finally speaks, He never gives one. He gives Himself. That is the answer the Bible offers to the why. Not an explanation. A presence.

The second wound is harder, and I want to sit in it with you, because I have been there. When someone you love dies, the felt sense of God often dies with them for a while. The prayers hit the ceiling. The songs at church feel like a language you used to speak. And the terror underneath is that maybe the felt presence was the whole thing, and now that it is gone, there was never anything there. I need you to hear this carefully. Feeling and faith are not the same organ. C.S. Lewis, who wrote A Grief Observed after his wife Joy died of cancer in 1960, described knocking on the door of God and hearing "a door slammed in your face, and a sound of bolting and double bolting on the inside. After that, silence." Lewis did not lose his faith in that book. But he learned that faith is not the warm feeling. Faith is what you do when the warm feeling leaves. The absence you feel is real. It is not the verdict on whether God is real.

Lewis noticed something in that grief that I have watched happen in dozens of grieving people, and it is worth naming so it does not frighten you. He found that the harder he tried to feel God, the more locked the door became, and that in his calmer moments, when he stopped clawing at the door in panic, something of God returned. Grief distorts. It makes you certain God has left precisely when you most need Him, the way a drowning man cannot tell which way is up. Do not trust the verdict your grief hands you about God's absence. Grief is a liar about many things, and this is the first thing it lies about. It tells you that because you cannot feel the floor, there is no floor. The floor is still there. You have simply lost, for now, the ability to feel it under you.

The empty tomb was also a place of grief

Christianity did not begin with people who avoided death. It began at a grave. And the first thing the risen Jesus said to Mary Magdalene, who was weeping outside the tomb because she thought His body had been stolen, was not a lecture. It was her name. "Jesus said to her, 'Mary'" (John 20:16). She did not recognize the resurrection in the abstract. She recognized it when He spoke her name in the dark, in her grief, before she understood anything. I have watched this happen at bedsides and gravesides for fifteen years. God rarely comes to the griever as an argument. He comes as a name spoken in the dark, a moment of unexpected mercy, a Scripture that lands, a friend who sat and said nothing. The resurrection is not a promise that death does not hurt. It is a promise that death does not win.

The tomb was empty, but Mary still wept before she knew it. Your tears are not evidence against the resurrection. They are the road to it.

And notice one more thing about that morning, because it matters for you. Mary was not comforted by the empty tomb. The empty tomb frightened her. She assumed grave robbers, not resurrection. The doctrine did not console her; the Person did. This is why I am wary of handing grieving people doctrine as though the right theology should function like a painkiller. It should not, and if it does, the grief was probably not real. What consoled Mary was not the proposition that resurrection is possible. It was Jesus, alive, speaking her name. I cannot promise you a felt encounter on a timeline. But I can tell you that in fifteen years I have watched God meet grieving people not with explanations but with Himself, in a moment they could not have manufactured, and that this is the pattern of the whole Bible. He does not send the griever a syllabus. He comes.

What to do with the silence

So what do you actually do, tonight, when the silence is loud. I will not give you a four-step plan, because grief does not run on plans and I refuse to insult your loss with a tidy box. But I will tell you what I have seen carry people through, as a pastor and as a man who has lost people I did not know how to live without.

Pray the anger. Do not wait until you feel reverent. The Psalms give you the words when you have none. Pray Psalm 88, which is the one lament in the whole book that never resolves, that ends in darkness, and God let it into the Scriptures anyway. He can hold your worst prayer. Stay near the ordinary means even when they feel dead. Keep going to the room where the people are, even when the songs feel like a foreign language, because grief lies to you about how long you have been alone, and the body of Christ is where the promise gets carried for you when you cannot carry it yourself. And find one person who will not fix you. Not a fixer. A sitter. The friends of Job got everything wrong the moment they opened their mouths, but for seven days they sat with him in silence, and that was the only thing they did right (Job 2:13).

And if the darkness has turned toward something more than grief, if you find yourself thinking you do not want to be here anymore, I need you to treat that as the emergency it is and not a spiritual failing. Call someone tonight. In the United States you can dial or text 988 and reach a person any hour. Tell your pastor, tell your doctor, tell someone who loves you. The God who wept at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35) does not want you to carry the weight alone, and neither do I.

The verdict I can give you

I cannot tell you why the person you love is gone. I have stopped pretending I can, and I have stopped trusting the pastors who claim they can. But I can tell you what I have staked my one life on, having come to it from unbelief and having tested it against the worst that death can do. The God of the Bible is not the God who explains suffering. He is the God who entered it. He did not send a memo about death. He went into the grave and came out the other side, and He did it so that the last word over the person you buried would not be the word death spoke.

Your doubt is not the end of your faith. It may be the labor pains of a faith that can finally survive the real world, the one where people you love actually die. The old faith, the one that needed everything to work out and everyone to stay, was always going to break on the first grave. Let it break. What is underneath it, if you will stay near the God who lets you weep in His presence, is older and harder and more able to carry you. Grief is not the proof that He left. It is, for now, the shape love takes when the person is gone. And love, the Scripture says, is strong as death (Song of Solomon 8:6). Stay near the One who is stronger.
excerpt: Grief does not argue with God. It goes quiet on Him. This is for the person whose faith did not survive the funeral in one piece.

title: Doubt After Being Abused by a Church Leader
body:
I want to be careful with the first words, because you have been handled carelessly by people who claimed to speak for God, and the last thing you need is another pastor being careless with you. So let me start here. What happened to you was not your fault. The man who used his position over you, whether the abuse was spiritual, emotional, sexual, or the cold cruelty of a system that protected him and discarded you, sinned against you and against God. Your doubt is not a spiritual weakness. It is the sane response of a soul that trusted the wrong hands.

The reason this doubt goes so deep is that the wound was not just personal. It was theological. When an ordinary person betrays you, you lose a person. When the man who stood in the pulpit and said "thus says the Lord" betrays you, you lose the pulpit, the Lord, and the possibility of trusting either one again. He did not just hurt you. He poisoned the well you were supposed to drink from. And now every time you try to pray, every time you hear a sermon, every time someone says the word God, his voice is there underneath it. That is not you being unforgiving. That is what abuse does. It attaches itself to the sacred so that you cannot reach for God without reaching through the man who hurt you.

God is angrier about this than you are

Here is something I need you to hear, and I need you to hear it from the whole weight of Scripture and not from my opinion. God is not on the side of the leader who abused you. He is furious about it. Jesus, who was the gentlest man who ever lived toward the broken, turned to iron when it came to those who damaged the vulnerable in His name. "Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to sin, it would be better for him to have a great millstone fastened around his neck and to be drowned in the depth of the sea" (Matthew 18:6). That is not a soft man. That is a Savior who would rather see the abuser weighted and thrown into the ocean than see him lay a hand on one of God's wounded.

And through the prophet Ezekiel, God pronounced judgment on the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves instead of the flock. "Ah, shepherds of Israel who have been feeding yourselves. Should not shepherds feed the sheep? You eat the fat, you clothe yourselves with the wool, you slaughter the fat ones, but you do not feed the sheep. The weak you have not strengthened, the sick you have not healed, the injured you have not bound up" (Ezekiel 34:2 through 4). Then God says the thing you need to hear. "Behold, I am against the shepherds" (Ezekiel 34:10). The God you are doubting stood against the man who hurt you before you ever thought to doubt.

The abuse told you God was on his side. The Scripture tells you God is against him. One of those is a lie, and it is not the one written in Ezekiel.

I want you to sit with the millstone verse, because I think you were taught to skip past the hard sayings of Jesus to get to the gentle ones, and this one was written for you. The Jesus who said "let the little children come to me" (Matthew 19:14) is the same Jesus who said He would rather see the one who harms them drowned in the depths of the sea. Those are not two different Jesuses. They are one Jesus, and His gentleness toward the vulnerable is the exact source of His ferocity toward those who prey on them. A love that did not turn to fury at the abuse of the beloved would not be love at all. It would be indifference. The God you are doubting is not indifferent to what happened to you. He is the opposite of indifferent. He is enraged on your behalf, and He has been enraged since before you found the words.

The lie of spiritual authority

Abusive church leaders almost always work the same con, and naming the mechanism can loosen its grip on your soul. They fuse themselves to God so that opposing them feels like opposing Him. They teach you that questioning them is questioning the Spirit, that submission to them is submission to Christ, that your discomfort is your rebellion. The scholar Diane Langberg, a psychologist who has spent more than fifty years working with trauma and abuse in the church, puts it plainly. Power in the church is meant to protect the vulnerable, and abuse is the use of that power to feed the self. She writes that abusers hide behind the very God they misrepresent. The man who hurt you wrapped himself in God so that when you finally pulled away, it would feel like you were pulling away from God Himself.

You need to separate those two things, and I know that is easier for me to write than for you to do. The man is not God. His voice is not God's voice. His misuse of Scripture is not what Scripture says. Jesus reserved His harshest words in the entire Gospels for religious leaders who loaded burdens on people and would not lift a finger to help (Matthew 23:4). The abuse you suffered is not the will of God. It is the exact thing Jesus came to overthrow.

Why deconversion feels like the only honest exit

I understand why many people in your position walk away entirely. If the church is where the wound happened, leaving the church feels like the only way to stop the bleeding. And I will not pull the cheap move of telling you to hurry back into the room where you were harmed. You may need distance. You may need years of distance. You may need a completely different congregation with real accountability before you can sit in a pew again without your body going cold. All of that can be true and you can still be walking with God.

But I want to name the thing that the abuser would love for you to believe, because it is his final victory. He would love for you to conclude that the whole thing is fraud, that there is no God behind the counterfeit he sold you, that the faith itself was the abuse. Hear me. A counterfeit is only possible where there is something real to counterfeit. Nobody forges leaves; they forge hundred dollar bills. The very fact that his fraud worked on you, that you were reaching for something true and holy and he exploited that reaching, tells you the true and holy thing exists. He could only steal from you because you were carrying something worth stealing.

Do not let the man who wounded you also get to define God for you forever. That would be his last and worst theft.

Where I have to be honest about the church

I cannot write this as a pastor and pretend my own house is clean. The American church has protected abusers. It has silenced victims. It has told women and children and vulnerable men to forgive and reconcile when what they needed was protection and justice. In 2019 the Houston Chronicle documented hundreds of cases of sexual abuse in Southern Baptist churches, and the pattern was not isolated evil but institutional cover. I am a Baptist pastor. That is my house. I do not get to wag a finger at the abuser and pretend the system I belong to did not build the walls he hid behind. We did this. Not only the man in your story. The structures that many of us kept comfortable, myself included, made room for him. If your doubt includes a verdict against the institutional church, some of that verdict is deserved, and I will not argue you out of a true thing.

What I will do is tell you that the failure of the church is not the failure of Christ. The two are not the same, though the abuser worked hard to make them feel identical. Jesus was betrayed by His own religious establishment. The Sanhedrin, the temple leadership, the men who held the sacred offices, handed Him over to be killed. If anyone had a right to conclude that the corruption of religious authority disproves God, it was the Man those authorities crucified. Instead He absorbed their betrayal into His own body and rose anyway. The church that failed you is not the last word. The One the church itself failed and killed and could not keep in the grave is.

The psychiatrist Judith Herman, whose 1992 book Trauma and Recovery remains one of the foundational texts on how people survive abuse, described the way trauma isolates its victims, cutting them off from the very community that could help them heal, and how healing requires the slow rebuilding of safe connection. This is worth naming because the abuser did to you spiritually what all abuse does relationally. He isolated you inside a distorted world where he defined reality, where your perceptions could not be trusted, where leaving felt like leaving God. Part of what you are experiencing as doubt is the disorientation of a person emerging from that constructed world and discovering that the map you were given was drawn by someone who profited from your confusion. It takes time to redraw the map. Be patient with yourself. You are not slow. You are recovering from something designed to keep you from recovering.

The question of forgiveness, handled honestly

Someone has almost certainly weaponized forgiveness against you already, so let me be precise, because the abuse of the concept is not the concept. You were probably told to forgive quickly, to reconcile, to move on, to not let bitterness take root, and that counsel was used to protect the abuser and silence you. Forgiveness in the Bible is not pretending the wrong did not happen. It is not restoring the abuser to a position of trust over you. It is not reconciliation without repentance. In Scripture, repentance precedes reconciliation, and there is no cheap grace that skips justice. Even Jesus, who told us to forgive, drove the money changers out of the temple with a whip of cords (John 2:15). You can, in time and never on anyone's schedule but your own, release the poison of vengeance from your soul, which is the mercy forgiveness offers the victim, without ever handing the abuser back the access he used to destroy you. Anyone who tells you real forgiveness requires returning to the site of your abuse is not quoting Scripture. They are protecting a predator with holy words, which is the very sin that put you here.

What healing might look like

I will not hand you a recovery timeline, because trauma does not run on schedules and the leaders who gave you formulas are part of why you are here. But I can tell you what I have watched God do in people who carried exactly your wound. Get to safety and get real help. This means putting distance between yourself and the abuser and the system that protected him, and it means finding a trauma-informed counselor, ideally one who understands both the psychology and the spiritual dimension of what religious abuse does. This is not a lack of faith. Naming the abuse to the proper authorities, including the police when a crime occurred, is not bitterness. It is justice, and God loves justice.

Then, when you are ready and not before, find people who reflect the real Jesus back to you. Not the counterfeit. A pastor who serves instead of consumes. A community with actual accountability, where the powerful are checked and the vulnerable are believed. Let the true thing slowly overwrite the false thing. And if the darkness turns toward not wanting to be here anymore, which happens more often after this kind of betrayal than people admit, please reach out tonight. In the United States you can call or text 988. Tell someone safe. You survived the abuse. Do not let it take the rest of you.

The verdict

The man who abused you lied to you about God. That is the deepest thing the abuse did, and it is the thing I most want to undo. He told you, with his position and his misused Scripture and his cruelty, that this is what God is like. He was wrong. God is the One who stands against the shepherds who eat the sheep. God is the One who would rather see a millstone around the abuser's neck than see him touch you. God is the One who was Himself betrayed by the religious establishment and killed by it and rose in spite of it.

Your doubt is not the end of your faith. It is your soul refusing to accept a counterfeit, and that refusal is holy. Do not let the man have the last word about God. He does not get to. That word belongs to the One he impersonated, and that One is looking at you with more tenderness and more fury on your behalf than you have let yourself imagine. You were sinned against. You are not forgotten. And the God the abuser hid behind is not hiding from you now.
excerpt: When the man who spoke for God is the one who wounded you, the wound goes all the way down. This is for the person the church betrayed.

title: Doubt After Studying Science
body:
I came to faith from atheism, and I want you to know that the version of atheism I held was not the lazy kind. I thought science had settled it. I thought the universe was a closed system of cause and effect, that evolution explained life without remainder, that the God hypothesis was a leftover from before we knew how anything worked, and that intelligent people had quietly stopped needing Him somewhere around the time we mapped the genome. So when I sit with someone whose faith cracked in a biology class or a physics lecture or a late night with a Richard Dawkins book, I am not sitting across from you. I am sitting where you are sitting, remembering the view.

Let me name the honest thing. Some of what shook your faith should have shaken it, because the faith you were handed was too small. If you were taught that the earth is six thousand years old, that evolution is a lie invented by atheists to destroy belief, that the fossil record is a trick, and that any Christian who reads Genesis differently has abandoned the Bible, then science did not disprove your faith. It disproved a bad theory about your faith that some well-meaning teacher handed you as though it were the faith itself. Those are not the same thing, and untangling them is most of the work.

The men who built modern science believed

Start with a fact that the popular story conveniently forgets. Modern science was not built by atheists rebelling against the church. It was largely built by Christians who believed the universe was orderly precisely because a rational God made it. Johannes Kepler, who gave us the laws of planetary motion, said he was thinking God's thoughts after Him. Isaac Newton wrote more about theology than about physics. Robert Boyle, the father of modern chemistry, funded lectures defending Christianity. Michael Faraday and James Clerk Maxwell, whose work on electromagnetism made your entire modern world possible, were serious believers. The sociologist and historian of science, whether you read Peter Harrison at Oxford or Rodney Stark, will tell you the same thing. The idea that science and Christianity are natural enemies is a nineteenth-century propaganda invention, popularized by John William Draper in 1874 and Andrew Dickson White in 1896, and historians of science abandoned it long ago even as it kept living in the popular imagination.

The war between science and faith is not a discovery of science. It is a story someone sold you, and the men who actually built the science did not believe it.

There is a deeper point buried in that history, and it is the one that eventually undid my atheism. Modern science assumes the universe is rationally intelligible, that its regularities can be captured in mathematical laws that the human mind can grasp. Why should that be true. Why should a universe produced by blind chance be comprehensible to the primate brains that evolved to find fruit and avoid predators. Einstein, no orthodox believer, admitted that the most incomprehensible thing about the universe is that it is comprehensible. The Christians who founded modern science had an answer. The universe is intelligible because a rational Mind made it, and He made human minds in His image, capable of thinking His thoughts after Him. Take God out of that picture and the intelligibility of the cosmos becomes a strange, unexplained gift that the science itself cannot account for. Science works. The question worth asking is why a godless universe should be the kind of place where science works at all.

What science can and cannot see

Here is the distinction that took me years to see, and once I saw it I could not unsee it. Science is stunningly good at answering one kind of question and structurally incapable of answering another. It tells you how the mechanism works. It cannot tell you why there is a mechanism at all, or what it is for, or whether your life means anything. Those are not gaps that better science will eventually fill. They are outside the tool.

Consider the question that has grown harder for atheism, not easier, over the last fifty years. Why is there something rather than nothing. And beyond that, why is the something so precisely tuned that it can hold life. The physicist Paul Davies, who is not a Christian apologist, has written extensively about the fine-tuning of the universe, the fact that the fundamental constants of physics sit within astonishingly narrow ranges that permit the existence of stars, chemistry, and living things. If the strong nuclear force were slightly different, if the cosmological constant were off by a factor most people cannot conceive, there would be no universe capable of containing anyone to notice. The atheist has answers to this, and I will not pretend the multiverse hypothesis is nonsense. But notice what has happened. The science did not close the door on God. It opened a stranger door than anyone expected, and reasonable people walk through it in both directions.

The point is not that science proves God. It does not, and any Christian who tells you the fine-tuning argument is a knockdown proof is overselling. The point is that the confident story, the one that says science ended the God question, is not what the frontier of science actually looks like. The frontier looks like awe and unanswered questions and physicists reaching for words like beautiful and improbable. Science handed us a universe more mysterious than the one that was supposed to explain God away.

The philosopher Antony Flew makes this point better than I can, because he was for half a century the most prominent academic atheist in the English-speaking world, the author of the papers that trained generations of philosophy students in unbelief. And in 2004, near the end of his life, he announced that he had come to believe in a God, not the God of the Bible, but a designing intelligence, and he said the evidence that moved him was precisely the science, the astonishing complexity of the genetic code and the fine-tuning of the constants. His book was called There Is a God. I do not offer him as a trump card. Flew was not a Christian and his conversion was to a bare theism, not to the cross. I offer him because he is proof that following the scientific evidence does not necessarily lead away from God, and that some of the sharpest minds who spent their lives arguing it did have ended up walking the other direction. The story that science settles the question against God is a story the science itself keeps failing to confirm.

Evolution and Genesis

Let me deal directly with the thing that shakes the most faith, because dodging it would be dishonest. The evidence for an old universe and for common descent is strong, and I am not going to ask you to pretend it is not. What I am going to ask you to reconsider is the assumption that this evidence contradicts the Bible. It contradicts one reading of the Bible, a reading that is younger than most people think. Young-earth creationism as a movement largely traces to the twentieth century, to the 1961 book The Genesis Flood by Henry Morris and John Whitcomb. Before that, many of the most conservative theologians read Genesis with far more flexibility. B.B. Warfield, the great defender of biblical inerrancy at Princeton in the early 1900s, accepted evolution as a possible means God used. Augustine, sixteen hundred years ago, warned Christians against reading Genesis in ways that make the faith look foolish to those who know the natural world, and he did not even have Darwin to worry about.

The question Genesis 1 answers is not the question your science textbook answers. Genesis was written to a people surrounded by pagan creation myths in which the world was made from the corpse of a slaughtered god and human beings were an afterthought made to be slaves. Against that, Genesis says one God spoke, the world is good, and human beings bear His image. It answers who and why. It was never trying to answer the mechanism, and demanding that it do so is a modern mistake pressed onto an ancient text. The biologist Francis Collins, who led the Human Genome Project and is one of the most accomplished scientists alive, is a serious Christian who sees no war between his lab and his faith. He wrote a book called The Language of God in 2006, and the title is the whole argument. He looks at the code of life and reads it as language, which is to say, as the work of a mind.

You did not have to choose between the microscope and the Maker. Someone told you that you did, and they were wrong on both counts.

The thing science cannot reach

Even if science explained every mechanism, from the first cell to the last synapse of your brain, it would not touch the questions that keep you awake. It cannot tell you that your children matter. It can describe the neurochemistry of love and never tell you whether love is real or an illusion the genes use to reproduce. It can explain the mechanism of grief and never tell you whether your grief is a tribute to something precious or a chemical accident to be medicated away. I have five sons. Science can tell me the biology of why I would run into a fire for them. It cannot tell me whether that instinct is nobility or delusion. Only a universe with meaning built into it can make my love for my sons anything more than a survival trick. The atheism I once held could not give me my own children as anything real. That, more than any argument, was the crack that let the light in.

What to actually do with the doubt

Read the Christians who know the science. Do not get your understanding of the debate from atheists describing believers, or from believers describing science they never studied. Read Francis Collins, read the physicist John Polkinghorne who was a Cambridge particle physicist before he was ordained, read the mathematician John Lennox at Oxford. You have been listening to one side narrate the other, and both sides do that badly. Then let the question sit without demanding it resolve tonight. Faith is not certainty about mechanisms. It is trust in a Person, held while many mechanisms remain unexplained. The apostle Paul knew nothing of quantum mechanics and staked his life on the resurrection of a man he had watched the church persecute and then met on a road (Acts 9).

The verdict

Science did not disprove God. It disproved a small god you were handed, a god who lived in the gaps of what we did not yet understand, and every good scientist should want that god gone, because he was never the God of the Bible. The God of the Bible is not the explanation for the lightning we have not yet figured out. He is the reason there is anything to figure out at all, the mind behind the order that makes science possible in the first place.

The telescope and the microscope did not make God smaller. They made Him larger than the Sunday school version you outgrew, and outgrowing that version was not a loss of faith. It was the beginning of one big enough to survive the actual universe, the one that is stranger and more beautiful and more precisely made than the flat story of your childhood ever let it be. Look through the lens again. The heavens are still declaring something (Psalm 19:1). The question is only whether you will let yourself hear it.
excerpt: You looked through the telescope and the microscope, and God got smaller. This is for the person who thinks the science ended the argument.

title: The Intellectual Doubter: When the Arguments Stop Working
body:
You are the reader I understand best, because you are the reader I was. You did not lose your faith to a scandal or a tragedy. You lost it to books. You started asking questions that your church treated as attacks, you went looking for answers, and the answers you found in most Christian apologetics were thin. They restated the conclusion as if it were a premise. They quoted the Bible to prove the Bible. They gave you certainty where the honest thing was probability, and your mind, which is not a defect but a gift, refused to pretend. So here you are, at the edge, unable to unread what you have read.

Let me say first what most pastors will not. Your questions are good questions. The problem of evil is a real problem. The hiddenness of God is a real difficulty. The historical distance between us and the events of the Gospels is real. The existence of sincere believers in other religions is a real challenge to any claim of exclusivity. If you were handed easy answers and found them hollow, you were not being faithless. You were being honest, and the answers were the problem, not your mind. The church has too often treated the sharpest minds as threats to be managed rather than gifts to be engaged, and it has driven away people it should have been begging to stay.

The arguments were never supposed to carry the whole weight

Here is the first thing I had to learn, coming from unbelief and expecting Christianity to be a system of airtight proofs. Christianity was never a conclusion you reason your way into with logical necessity. Nobody in the New Testament believed because a syllogism forced them to. They believed because they encountered a Person, saw an empty tomb, met witnesses who would not recant under torture, and found that the whole thing made sense of their lives in a way nothing else did. The arguments matter. They can clear obstacles, and I have spent my life on them. But they were never designed to compel belief the way a mathematical proof compels agreement. If you were told that the arguments should force the conclusion and then found they did not, you were told something false about how faith works, even for the most rigorous believer.

The mathematician and philosopher Blaise Pascal, who was one of the great scientific minds of the seventeenth century, saw this three hundred and fifty years ago. He wrote that "the heart has its reasons which reason does not know," and he did not mean that faith is irrational sentiment. He meant that the deepest kinds of knowing, the knowing of persons, the knowing of beauty, the knowing that your own existence is worth something, do not run entirely through the proof-generating part of the mind. You know your spouse loves you, but you cannot prove it to a skeptic the way you prove the Pythagorean theorem. That is not a defect in the knowledge. It is the nature of knowing a person rather than a proposition.

You have been trying to reach a Person with a proof. The proof was never going to get you there, and the failure of the proof is not the absence of the Person.

I do not say this to smuggle in irrationalism, and I want to guard against that misreading because you are exactly the reader who would catch it. I am not telling you to stop thinking and start feeling. I am telling you that the tool you have been using, deductive proof, is the wrong tool for the object, and a wrong tool failing does not mean the object is not there. You do not prove a historical event the way you prove a theorem; you weigh the evidence and reach a judgment of probability, the way a jury does, the way a historian does, the way you do when you conclude that Julius Caesar existed though you cannot prove it with the certainty of arithmetic. Christianity is a historical claim about a Person and an empty tomb. It asks for the kind of assent you give to well-attested history, not the kind you give to mathematics. If you demanded mathematical certainty and were disappointed, you demanded of the faith something the faith never claimed to give, and something you demand of nothing else you believe.

Doubt your doubts

The philosopher and pastor Tim Keller made an observation in The Reason for God in 2008 that reoriented my thinking, and I offer it to you not as a trick but as a discipline you owe your own honesty. Every doubt is built on a belief. When you doubt Christianity because of the suffering in the world, you are standing on a belief that suffering is genuinely evil, that the world ought to be otherwise, that there is a way things are supposed to be. Where did you get that. A purely material universe, atoms colliding without purpose, has no oughts in it. Suffering just is; it is not wrong. The very outrage that fuels your doubt is smuggling in a moral framework that materialism cannot supply. So the honest doubter has to turn the blade both ways. Do not only doubt the faith. Doubt the beliefs your doubts are standing on. Ask whether your alternative can actually account for the moral seriousness with which you reject Christianity.

I am not doing a sleight of hand here. I am asking you to apply the same rigor to your unbelief that you applied to your belief. When I did that, honestly, I found that the atheism I held could not account for the things I was most certain of. That my reason was reliable, when it was supposedly produced by a blind process selected for survival and not for truth. That morality was real, when it was supposedly a useful illusion. That my life meant something, when the universe supposedly did not care whether I or my children lived or died. The intellectual doubter prides himself on following the evidence. Follow it all the way. Ask what it costs your unbelief to be true, and whether you can actually live there.

The evidence you may have skipped

Because you are an intellectual doubter, you deserve intellectual honesty about where the strongest case actually is, and it is not where popular apologetics usually points. The strongest historical case for Christianity is the resurrection, and it is stronger than most doubters realize because most doubters have only heard it dismissed, never examined. The historian and New Testament scholar N.T. Wright wrote an eight-hundred-page work called The Resurrection of the Son of God in 2003, arguing as a historian, not a preacher, that the rise of the early church is a historical event that demands a historical explanation. Something happened that turned terrified, defeated followers of an executed teacher into people who proclaimed His resurrection in the very city where He was killed, weeks later, and went to their deaths refusing to recant. The atheist New Testament scholar Bart Ehrman grants that the earliest followers sincerely believed they had seen Jesus alive. The disagreement is about what to make of that, not whether it happened. That is a much narrower disagreement than you may have been led to believe.

You do not have to find the resurrection persuasive tonight. I am asking something smaller. I am asking you to make sure that the version of the case you rejected was the strong version and not the cartoon. Most intellectual doubters, in my experience, rejected the cartoon, the version they got in a youth group, and then read atheists who were also arguing against the cartoon, and never once encountered the case at its strongest. That is not following the evidence. That is following the caricature.

Let me push on one specific thing, because it moved me and it may move you. The earliest followers of Jesus had every reason not to invent a resurrection. They were Jews, and Jewish resurrection hope was about the general resurrection at the end of history, all the righteous raised together on the last day. Nobody expected one man to rise in the middle of history, alone, ahead of everyone else. It was not a category they possessed. When the disciples claimed Jesus had risen, they were asserting something their own theology had no slot for, in the city where He was executed, weeks after His public death, to a hostile establishment that could have produced the body and ended the movement in an afternoon. And they did not stop when it cost them their lives. People die for what they sincerely believe true all the time. It is much rarer for people to die for what they know to be a lie they themselves fabricated. Something happened. The honest doubter owes it to his own honesty to reckon with what.

Reject the strongest form of Christianity if you must. But make sure it is the strongest form you are rejecting, and not the version a nervous youth pastor handed you at fifteen.

The danger of the intellectual position

I have to name a temptation, and I name it as someone who has fallen into it. The intellectual doubter can hide inside the doubt. Perpetual questioning can become a way of never having to commit, never having to be wrong, never having to submit your life to anything larger than your own mind. It feels like rigor. It can be cowardice wearing the mask of rigor. At some point the honest thing is not more reading. It is a decision, made in the face of evidence that will never be complete, the way every important decision in a human life is made. You did not wait for a proof before you married. You did not wait for a proof before you had children, if you did. You acted on sufficient evidence and committed, because that is what adults do with the questions that matter most, and no important question ever comes with a proof attached.

The verdict

The arguments stopped working because you were asking them to do a job they were never built to do. They were never meant to carry you all the way to God by logical force. They were meant to clear the road so that you could meet Him. And the reason the popular arguments felt thin is that many of them were thin, offered by people more interested in winning than in truth. Your dissatisfaction with them is not a mark against your faith. It is a mark of your seriousness, and God is not afraid of serious people. He made your mind.

Stay in the questions, but stop hiding in them. Doubt your doubts as rigorously as you doubted your faith. Read the strongest case, not the cartoon. And know that the God you are reasoning toward is not a conclusion at the end of an argument. He is a Person who has been standing at the edge of your reasoning the whole time, waiting for you to stop trying to prove Him and start looking for Him. "You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:13). Not with all your certainty. With all your heart. The mind is invited. It was just never going to be the thing that carried you across.
excerpt: You read your way to the edge of faith and the arguments you were given did not hold. This is for the honest mind that cannot pretend.

title: The Emotional Doubter: When God Feels Absent
body:
Your doubt is not the intellectual kind, and that is why it is so lonely. You are not troubled by the problem of evil or the historicity of the Gospels. You could probably win the argument. That is what makes it worse. Because when you get on your knees, there is nothing there. The prayers go up and stop at the ceiling. The songs at church that used to move you now sound like words you are mouthing to be polite. God, who was once so near you could almost feel His breath, has gone silent, and no argument can touch a silence. You do not doubt that He exists. You doubt that He is here, with you, and increasingly you doubt that He was ever as near as you once believed.

I need to tell you at the outset that this is one of the most well-documented experiences in the entire history of Christian devotion, and the fact that nobody told you about it is a failure of the modern church, not a sign that something is wrong with your soul. The tradition has a name for what you are in. It is old, it is honored, and the greatest saints walked through it. You are not falling out of faith. You may be walking through a country that the deepest believers who ever lived also crossed.

The dark night has a mapmaker

In sixteenth-century Spain, a Carmelite friar named John of the Cross was imprisoned by his own religious order, held in a cell barely large enough to lie down in, beaten weekly. In that darkness he wrote about a spiritual condition he called the dark night of the soul. And here is the part that will surprise you if you have only heard the phrase used casually. John did not describe the dark night as a spiritual failure or a season of sin. He described it as a work of God. He argued that God withdraws the felt sense of His presence on purpose, to wean the soul off spiritual feelings and teach it to love God for Himself rather than for the pleasant sensations of belief. The beginner, John said, loves the consolations of God. The mature soul must learn to love the God of the consolations even when the consolations are gone. And the only way to learn that is to have them taken away.

Read that again if you need to. The absence you are experiencing, in this ancient reading, is not God leaving. It is God maturing you past the stage of needing to feel Him constantly, the stage of a spiritual infant. It feels like abandonment. It may be the most intimate thing He has ever done, because He only does it to souls He is taking somewhere.

The felt presence of God was the milk of your infancy. Its removal is not starvation. It may be the beginning of solid food.

Understand what John was diagnosing, because the modern misuse of his phrase has hidden it. He distinguished between two darknesses, the night of the senses and the deeper night of the spirit, and he insisted that in both, the darkness was purgative, not punitive. God was not angry. God was refining. When a lover first falls in love, everything is feeling, all warmth and fire. But a mature love is proven precisely in the seasons when the feeling is absent and the commitment holds anyway. John argued that God, wanting to bring the soul into that mature love, must at some point remove the fire so that the soul learns to love the Beloved and not merely the warmth the Beloved provides. It is the most counterintuitive thing in Christian spirituality. The withdrawal is the gift. The soul just cannot see it while it is inside the dark, any more than a seed can see the point of being buried.

Mother Teresa spent fifty years here

When Mother Teresa's private letters were published in 2007 in the book Come Be My Light, the world was stunned, and many atheists claimed it as proof she had secretly been a fraud. Read them and you will find the opposite. For nearly fifty years, from around 1949 until her death, the woman who served the dying in the streets of Calcutta, the woman whose face became the world's picture of holiness, felt almost nothing of God. She wrote of "such deep longing for God" and then "such terrible separation." She wrote, "the place of God in my soul is blank. There is no God in me." She wrote to her spiritual director in agony, wondering if her whole life of faith had been a lie.

And here is what you must not miss. She kept serving. She kept praying into the silence. She got up every morning for five decades and loved the poorest of the poor for a God she could not feel. Her spiritual directors eventually helped her understand her darkness as a participation in the very abandonment Christ felt on the cross, a way of being united to the Jesus who cried out "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me" (Matthew 27:46). The most famous believer of the twentieth century lived her whole public ministry inside the exact absence you are describing, and it did not falsify her faith. It deepened it into something almost unbearable and almost unbearably beautiful. If the felt presence of God were the measure of real faith, Mother Teresa had less of it than the average churchgoer on a good Sunday. Clearly the felt presence is not the measure.

Faith is not a feeling, and this is a mercy

Here is the trap that modern Christianity built for you, and I have to name it because it is doing you real harm. Much of the contemporary church, especially in its worship and its language, has quietly taught that the presence of God is a feeling, that a good spiritual life produces emotional highs, that if you are close to God you will feel close to God. This is not in the Bible. It is a product of a therapeutic culture that measures everything by how it makes us feel, and it set you up for a fall the moment the feelings faded. Because feelings always fade. They are weather, not climate. And a faith built on weather cannot survive a drought.

The biblical picture of faith is not a feeling but a covenant. It is a marriage, and any honest married person knows that the feeling of being in love comes and goes across the years, sometimes for long stretches, while the marriage itself, the commitment, the daily faithfulness, holds underneath. I have been married long enough to know the difference between the feeling and the vow, and I know which one carried us through the years when the feeling was thin. Your faith is in a dry season of feeling. The vow is still there. God's faithfulness does not fluctuate with your emotional weather. "If we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself" (2 Timothy 2:13). Read that slowly. Even your faithlessness does not change His faithfulness. He is not holding on to you because you feel Him. He is holding on to you because that is who He is.

You are treating a feeling as if it were the foundation. The feeling was always the weather. The foundation is a covenant, and it is holding whether you feel it or not.

I have to indict my own tradition here, because the wound you are carrying was partly manufactured by the church that formed you. We built worship services engineered to produce feeling, we measured spiritual health by emotional response, we told new believers that the warmth of their conversion was the presence of God rather than the excitement of a new love, and we never once prepared them for the morning the warmth would not come. So when it did not come, they had no framework except the terrible conclusion that God had left or was never there. We did this. I have led services designed to move people and called the movement the Spirit, and I have had to repent of teaching people to trust a feeling I could manufacture with the right song in the right key. The saints of the church knew better for two thousand years. We forgot it in about two generations, and you are paying the price for our forgetting.

What to do inside the silence

Do not try to manufacture the feeling back. This is the mistake most people make, and it deepens the despair, because when the manufactured feeling fails they conclude they are beyond hope. Stop chasing the sensation. Instead, do what Mother Teresa did and what John of the Cross prescribed. Keep the practices even when they feel empty. Keep praying, even if the prayer is only the words of the Psalms read into the dark. Keep going to the room where the people gather, even when the songs feel like a foreign language, because the body of Christ carries the faith for you when you cannot feel it, and there is a mercy in being carried. Keep serving someone poorer than you, because Christ said He is found among the least (Matthew 25:40), and you may meet in the face of the suffering the God you cannot find in your feelings.

And I have to say the pastoral thing plainly, because the dark night and clinical depression can look identical from the inside and they are not the same and they can also occur together. If the absence you feel comes with a loss of the will to live, with a darkness that is closing off every door, please do not treat that as merely a spiritual condition to be prayed through alone. See a doctor. Tell someone who loves you. In the United States you can call or text 988 tonight and reach a person. God works through medicine and through counselors and through the hand of a friend, and reaching for that help is not a failure of faith. It is faith taking the next faithful step.

The verdict

The silence is real. I will not talk you out of it or tell you that you are imagining it or hand you a technique to make God feel close by Friday. The saints who felt it most were the ones closest to Him, which should tell you the silence is not the abandonment it pretends to be. God is not gone. He has, for reasons you cannot see now and may not see for years, withdrawn the feeling of His nearness, and He has done it to souls He was taking somewhere deep. You are in good and holy company in the dark.

Keep walking through it the way Teresa did, one faithful morning at a time, loving a God you cannot feel because you decided long ago that He was worth loving whether or not He made you feel good. That decision, held in the dark, is not a lesser faith than the felt kind. It is a greater one. It is the faith that survives the removal of everything except the naked will to keep trusting. And on the far side of the dark night, the tradition promises and the saints testify, there is a union with God that the beginner's warm feelings could never have reached. The silence is not the end of your faith. It may be the making of it. Hold on.
excerpt: The arguments are fine. It is the silence that is killing you. This is for the believer whose God has gone quiet.

title: Doubt in Leadership: When the Pastor Doesn't Believe
body:
I am going to speak to you as one pastor to another, because I suspect you have not been able to say this out loud to anyone, and the isolation is part of what is killing you. You stand up on Sunday and you proclaim things you are no longer sure you believe. You pray over the sick and you wonder if anyone is listening. You counsel a couple to trust God through their crisis and you drive home doubting the God you told them to trust. And you cannot tell a soul, because your doubt is not just a private struggle. It is a professional catastrophe. Your salary, your housing, your identity, your family's stability, your entire life is built on the assumption that you believe. So you carry it alone, and it is crushing you, and every Sunday you feel more like a fraud.

I want to say something before anything else, because you need to hear it from someone who understands the specific weight you carry. You are not the first pastor to stand in a pulpit uncertain of the words. You are in a long and honest line. And your doubt does not make you a hypocrite. A hypocrite is someone who does not believe and does not care. You are a person who wants to believe, who is agonizing precisely because you take the truth seriously. That agony is the opposite of hypocrisy. It is integrity fighting for its life.

The unique isolation of the doubting leader

Every doubter is lonely, but you carry a loneliness with a special cruelty. The ordinary believer who doubts can go to their pastor. You are the pastor.
