You are the one everyone else brings their doubts to, which means when the doubt is yours, you have nowhere to bring it. The system that was built to catch struggling believers has no place for the struggling shepherd, because we built a church culture that expects its leaders to have already arrived, to be past the questions, to be certainties on legs. That expectation is unbiblical and it is destroying good pastors, and I say we built it because I am part of the profession that built it.

Consider the men God actually used to lead His people. Moses argued with God and tried to refuse the call, insisting he was inadequate (Exodus 4). Elijah, right after the greatest triumph of his ministry, collapsed under a broom tree and asked God to let him die (1 Kings 19:4). Jeremiah, the weeping prophet, accused God to His face: "O Lord, you have deceived me, and I was deceived" (Jeremiah 20:7). John the Baptist, who had baptized Jesus and heard the voice from heaven, sent messengers from prison to ask, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?" (Matthew 11:3). The forerunner of Christ doubted whether Christ was the Christ. If your ministry disqualifies you for doubting, then it disqualified the entire prophetic tradition and half the leaders in the Bible.

The Scriptures did not give us leaders who never doubted. They gave us doubters God used anyway, and then we invented a ministry culture that would have run every one of them out of the building.

There is a particular cruelty in the way the profession is structured, and I have felt it in my own bones. A doctor who gets sick can be treated. A therapist in crisis can see another therapist. But a pastor whose faith is failing has no obvious place to go, because the entire apparatus assumes the pastor is the strong one, the settled one, the one others lean on. We are the emergency room that is not allowed to have patients. And so the doubting pastor learns to perform belief he does not feel, week after week, and the gap between the public self in the pulpit and the private self in the study grows into a chasm that can swallow a man whole. That chasm, not the doubt itself, is what destroys pastors. The doubt is survivable. The years of pretending are not. What you cannot sustain is the split.

Get honest about which doubt this is

You need to diagnose your doubt, because different doubts need different responses, and the fog you are in makes them all feel the same. Let me name the kinds I have seen in fellow pastors, myself included.

Sometimes the doubt is exhaustion wearing the mask of unbelief. You are burned out. You have poured yourself out for years, you are running on empty, and a depleted soul cannot feel God and mistakes the numbness for atheism. Elijah under the broom tree did not need a theology lecture. He needed sleep and food, which is exactly what God gave him before speaking a single word (1 Kings 19:5 through 8). If you have not rested in years, your doubt may be your body sending a bill you have refused to pay. Sometimes the doubt is intellectual, real questions you were never allowed to ask in seminary or in your tradition, questions you buried to get ordained and that have surfaced now with interest. Sometimes it is the dark night, the withdrawal of felt presence that the deepest saints walked through. And sometimes, in honesty, it is genuine deconstruction, a real erosion of belief that needs to be faced and not managed. You cannot treat what you have not named. The first work is not to fix the doubt. It is to look at it clearly and ask what it actually is.

The integrity question you cannot avoid

I have to be a pastor to you here and not just a comfort, because you know as well as I do that there is an integrity question underneath this, and dodging it will rot you from the inside. You are being paid to represent something. If you have moved from doubt to settled unbelief, from struggling with the faith to no longer holding it, then continuing to preach it for a paycheck is a wound to your own soul that no amount of rationalization will heal. I am not saying this to threaten you. I am saying it because you already feel it, and naming it is the first mercy.

But hear the distinction carefully, because it is the whole thing. There is a vast difference between preaching what you doubt and preaching what you disbelieve. To preach while struggling, while wrestling, while holding on by your fingernails to a faith you cannot currently feel, is not fraud. It is what faithful ministry has always partly been. Charles Spurgeon, the greatest preacher of the Victorian age, battled crippling depression his whole life and preached through it. Martin Luther was tormented by seasons of what he called Anfechtungen, spiritual assaults so severe he thought he was damned, and he pastored the whole Reformation from inside them. To preach while doubting is to preach as a wounded healer, and the church has always needed those more than it needed the falsely certain. But to preach while settled in unbelief, having quietly decided the whole thing is false and continuing for the salary and the status, is a different matter, and your own conscience is the one telling you so. The question is not whether you doubt. It is which side of that line you are on, and only you and God know.

Preaching through doubt is faithfulness. Preaching through settled unbelief is a slow death of the soul. You already know which one you are doing. Stop pretending you do not.

I want to add one thing to that line, because pastors are experts at self-condemnation and I do not want to hand you a new whip. Most doubting pastors are not on the wrong side of that line. They fear they are, which is itself evidence they are not, because a man who has genuinely abandoned the faith does not lie awake in anguish about whether he still holds it. The very torment you feel is your faith fighting, and a faith that fights is a faith that lives. Do not let the fear that you might be a fraud convince you that you are one. Test it honestly, before God and one trusted person, but do not let the accusation win by default. Most of the men I have walked through this were far closer to God than they believed, and they nearly threw away a true calling because they mistook a dark season for a settled apostasy. Do not make that mistake in haste.

What you actually need to do

Break the isolation, safely. You need one person, outside your congregation and outside your chain of authority, to whom you can tell the whole truth. A pastor of pastors. A spiritual director. A counselor who understands ministry. A trusted friend in another city who will not report you to your board. The Pastors Connection Network exists in part for exactly this, because I built it knowing how alone this work can make a man. The doubt grows in the dark and shrinks in the light, and the single most dangerous thing about your situation is that you have kept it in the dark. Say it out loud to one safe person this week.

Then rest and rebuild before you decide anything. Do not make a life-altering decision about your calling from inside exhaustion. If you are burned out, the doubt may lift substantially once you are not running on empty, and you will thank God you did not resign in the fog. Take the sabbatical. Take the leave. If your church will not give it, that is information about the church, not about God. And do the honest theological work you have been too busy or too afraid to do, with people who will not fire you for asking. Some pastors, doing this work, find their faith deepens into something far more durable than the untested certainty they had before. Some conclude they need to step out of vocational ministry with integrity, and that too can be a faithful act. What you cannot do is stay indefinitely in the fog, preaching by momentum, hoping it resolves itself. It will not. It will only cost you more.

And I will say to you what I say to every doubter, because pastors are not exempt from the dark places and are in fact more prone to them. If the weight has turned toward not wanting to be here anymore, if you have thought that everyone would be better off without you, that lie has taken more ministers than the church admits. Reach out tonight. Call or text 988 in the United States. Tell your safe person. Your congregation needs a living, honest, struggling pastor far more than they need a perfect one, and infinitely more than they need to bury one.

The verdict

You are not a fraud. You are a shepherd in the dark, and the church built no place for you, and that is our sin, not yours. The men God used to lead His people were doubters and depressives and arguers and men who begged to die. You are in the line, not outside it. But you cannot stay in the fog forever, preaching by muscle memory, hoping no one notices the cost. Name the doubt. Break the isolation. Rest before you decide. And face the integrity question honestly, not with fear but with the courage that made you a pastor in the first place.

Ministry does not require that you never doubt. It requires that you be honest before God about the doubt, that you fight for the faith rather than quietly abandon it while cashing the check, and that you love the people in front of you enough to get well. The God you are unsure of tonight called doubting men and used them mightily, and He has not stopped. He is not surprised by your doubt. He is not disgusted by it. He is waiting for you to stop carrying it alone, because you were never meant to, and least of all in this. Come out of the dark. There is more grace in the light than the isolation let you believe.
excerpt: You preach it on Sunday and you are not sure you believe it. This is for the leader carrying a secret that could end everything.

title: Doubt After Tragedy
body:
Something happened that should not have happened. A child's diagnosis. A drunk driver. A diagnosis that came back and then came back worse. A shooting. A disaster that took people who had done nothing to deserve it. And somewhere in the wreckage, your faith broke, because the God you believed in was supposed to prevent exactly this, and He did not. The doubt after tragedy is not academic. It is a specific and burning accusation. Where were You. You could have stopped it. You did not. And no clever argument reaches the place where that accusation lives.

I will not begin with a defense of God. He does not need me to be His lawyer, and you do not need another Christian rushing to protect God from your pain. I begin instead by agreeing with you about the size of the wound. What happened was genuinely evil, genuinely senseless, genuinely wrong. The Bible does not ask you to pretend otherwise. It does not ask you to call the tragedy a blessing in disguise or a lesson or part of a plan you should be grateful for. Anyone who told you that added cruelty to your grief. The tragedy was tragic. Starting anywhere else is a lie, and I refuse to lie to you.

The Bible screams too

Here is what stunned me, coming to Scripture from atheism, expecting a book of easy comfort. The Bible contains the exact accusation you are making, on the lips of its most faithful people, and God does not strike them down for it. The prophet Habakkuk stood before God and demanded, "O Lord, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? Or cry to you 'Violence' and you will not save? Why do you make me see iniquity, and why do you idly look at wrong?" (Habakkuk 1:2 through 3). That is a book of the Bible. That is not a doubter outside the faith. That is a prophet inside it, screaming your exact scream, and God receives it.

The whole book of Job is one long protest against undeserved suffering. Job loses his children, his health, his wealth, everything, for reasons he never learns, and he spends thirty-eight chapters refusing to accept the pious explanations his friends offer him. And when God finally speaks, the astonishing thing is that God sides with Job against the friends. "You have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7). The friends defended God with tidy theology. Job accused God with honest anguish. And God preferred the honest accusation to the dishonest defense. Let that reach you. Your raw protest may be closer to real faith than the neat answers people have been handing you.

God preferred Job's furious honesty to his friends' comfortable theology. Your accusation may be nearer to Him than the platitudes you have been offered.

Consider what this does to the popular idea that faith means never questioning God. That idea is not biblical. It is a folk religion of politeness, and it has nothing to do with the God of Job and Habakkuk and the Psalms and the crucified Christ who screamed a question from the cross. The Scriptures are full of people who took God to court, who filed their grievances loudly, who refused to be talked out of the reality of their pain by well-meaning friends. And God, over and over, honors them for it. The one thing He will not abide is the false comfort, the pious lie, the friend who defends God by minimizing the suffering. If your doubt is a refusal to pretend the tragedy was fine, then your doubt is on the side of Job, and Job is the one God vindicated. You are not being unfaithful by refusing to make peace with the wrong. You are being honest, and the Scriptures make room for exactly that honesty.

The answer God gives is not an explanation

You want to know why. I understand, because I have wanted to know why at gravesides I will never forget. And I have to be honest with you about what the Bible does and does not offer here, because false advertising would only deepen the wound later. When God finally answers Job, He does not explain. Job never learns about the conversation in the heavens that opened the book. God does not give Job the reason. Instead, for four chapters, God takes Job on a tour of the wildness and vastness of creation, the ostrich and the storm and the great sea creatures, and the effect is not to answer Job's question but to enlarge Job's frame. God essentially says, there is more going on in this universe than you can see from where you stand, and you are going to have to trust that I am good in the parts you cannot see.

That is not a satisfying answer if you want the mechanics of your particular tragedy explained. It is a different kind of answer. It is the answer of a Person rather than a formula. And notice what Job does with it. He does not get his explanation. He gets God. "I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you" (Job 42:5). The tragedy did not get explained. God got closer. For Job, that turned out to be the thing he actually needed, though he did not know it when he was demanding the explanation.

The God who did not stay at a safe distance

Here is where Christianity says something no other worldview says, and it is the thing that finally held me when the arguments could not. The Christian God did not explain suffering from a throne at a safe distance. He entered it. The center of the Christian faith is not a philosophy of why bad things happen. It is a bleeding man on a Roman cross. When you accuse God of allowing senseless suffering, Christianity's response is to point at Golgotha and say, He knows. He was tortured to death by an unjust system while the innocent watched. God is not the distant deity who permits tragedy from above. In Christ, He is the one who climbed down into the worst of it and let it fall on Himself.

The theologian Jurgen Moltmann was a young German soldier in World War Two, taken prisoner, and it was in the prison camp, confronting the horror his own nation had committed and the suffering all around him, that he came to faith. He later wrote The Crucified God in 1972, and his argument was that the only God worth believing in after the atrocities of the twentieth century is a God who suffers, a God on the cross, a God who does not stand outside human agony but enters it. A God who merely permitted suffering while remaining untouched by it would be a monster. The God of the cross is not that God. He is the God who was crucified. Whatever your tragedy is, He is not watching it from outside. He carries a wound too.

An untouched God who merely allows tragedy would deserve your accusation. The crucified God, who climbed into the worst of it, deserves your attention.

The novelist and survivor Elie Wiesel, who lived through Auschwitz and lost his family there, wrote in his memoir Night about watching the Nazis hang a young boy, a child too light to die quickly, who strangled slowly on the gallows while the camp was forced to watch. Wiesel wrote that a man behind him whispered, where is God now, and something in Wiesel answered, He is here, hanging on this gallows. Wiesel meant it as the death of his faith, the moment God died for him in the camps, and I will not steal his meaning or baptize his grief; he was not a Christian and his loss was real and his own. But a Christian cannot read that line without a strange recognition, because the Christian claim is precisely that God is on the gallows, that when a child dies unjustly God is not comfortable in heaven but is Himself the crucified one, hanging with the innocent. Wiesel intended a verdict against God. The gospel takes the same image and says, yes, and that is the only God worth having, the one who is on the gallows with the boy.

What faith looks like in the wreckage

So what do you do, actually, when the tragedy has broken your faith and no answer reaches the pain. I will not give you steps, because tragedy shatters steps and I will not insult your loss with a tidy plan. But I can tell you what I have watched carry people through the unbearable.

Pray the protest. Do not wait until you can pray something reverent. Pray Habakkuk. Pray Job. Pray the psalm that asks "how long, O Lord?" (Psalm 13:1). God has proven He can hold your accusation without flinching, so give it to Him instead of letting it fester in the dark where it turns to poison. Let people carry you. The friends of Job ruined everything the moment they spoke, but for seven days they sat with him in silence, and that was the one thing they did right (Job 2:13). Find the sitters. Avoid the explainers. And do not demand that your faith resolve on a timeline. The resolution, if it comes, will not come as an answer to the why. It will come, if it comes, as a presence in the dark, the sense that you are not carrying this alone, the God who was crucified drawing near to a wound He knows from the inside.

And I have to say the thing I say to every person in the dark places, because tragedy drives people there more than almost anything. If the grief has turned toward not wanting to be here anymore, please treat that as the emergency it is. Reach out tonight. In the United States you can call or text 988. Tell someone who loves you. The God who wept at a tomb (John 11:35) does not want you to face the darkness alone, and neither do the people who love you.

The verdict

I cannot tell you why the tragedy happened. I have stopped pretending any pastor can, and I have learned to distrust the ones who claim to know. What I can tell you is that your accusation against God is not outside the faith. It is written into the Scriptures, on the lips of prophets and sufferers God vindicated. Your protest is not the end of your faith. It may be, as it was for Job, the strange beginning of actually seeing Him.

The tragedy is real and it is wrong and it is not explained. But the God you are accusing is not the safe and distant deity you thought you were losing. He is the God with wounds, the one who did not send an answer down to your suffering but came down into it, the one who was broken by an evil He could have stopped and let it fall on Himself so that evil would not have the final word. Your faith did not break because it was false. It broke because it was too small to hold the real world, the one where tragedies actually happen. Let the small faith break. What is underneath it, the crucified God who knows your wound from the inside, is the only faith strong enough to hold what you are carrying. Stay near Him in the dark. He is nearer than the silence lets you feel.
excerpt: The senseless thing happened, and your faith could not hold the weight of it. This is for the person the world broke.

title: The Married Doubter: When One Spouse Loses Faith
body:
You built a life on a shared faith, and now that foundation has shifted. Maybe you are the one who has lost your faith, watching your spouse's hurt and confusion and fear, feeling like a stranger in your own marriage, wondering if the person who married you can still love the person you are becoming. Or maybe you are the one still believing, watching your husband or wife walk away from the God you built your home around, feeling abandoned in a way that has no name, grieving a person who is still sitting across the dinner table. Either way, something you assumed would always be shared has become the thing that divides you, and the marriage is straining under a weight neither of you planned for.

I want to be careful here, because both of you are hurting and the church usually only speaks to one of you. It tells the believing spouse to stand firm and pray, and it tells the doubting spouse, implicitly or explicitly, that they are the problem. I am not going to do that. I am going to speak to both people in this marriage, because there are two souls in this story, and both of them are afraid, and both of them deserve better than the sides they are being pushed onto.

To the spouse who still believes

Your grief is real, and I want to name it before I say anything else, because most people around you are treating this as a theological problem to be solved rather than a loss to be mourned. You are grieving. The person you married, the one you dreamed with about raising your children in the faith, about growing old in the same pew, about a shared eternity, has changed in the one way you never prepared for. That is a genuine bereavement, even though they are still alive and still yours. Do not let anyone rush you past the grief or shame you for feeling it.

But I have to give you a warning, gently, because I have watched believing spouses lose their marriages not to the doubt but to their response to the doubt. The temptation is to turn your marriage into a mission field. To argue. To leave apologetics books on the nightstand. To turn every conversation into an altar call. To make your spouse a project. I understand the impulse. It comes from love and from fear. But it does not work, and worse, it often drives the doubting spouse further away, because now they do not just doubt God, they feel judged and cornered by the person who is supposed to love them most. The apostle Peter addressed exactly this situation, married believers with unbelieving spouses, and his counsel is stunning. He said the unbelieving spouse may be won "without a word" by the conduct of the believer (1 Peter 3:1). Without a word. Not by argument. By a life so full of grace that it makes the faith attractive rather than defensive. Your job is not to win the debate. Your job is to love your spouse so well that your faith becomes the most compelling thing in the house.

You cannot argue your spouse back to God. But you can love them in a way that makes God look real. Choose the second. The first has buried more marriages than it has saved.

There is a fear underneath your grief that you may not have named, and I want to name it for you so it stops working in the dark. You are afraid that if you stop pushing, you are giving up on your spouse's soul, that gentleness is a betrayal of the truth, that a loving God requires you to fight harder for their return. Hear me carefully. The pressure you feel to save your spouse is not from God. God is not anxious. He is not wringing His hands hoping you will land the right argument before it is too late. Your spouse's soul is not finally in your hands; it is in His, and He loves them more than you do, which is a sentence worth sitting with because it is almost impossible to believe when you love someone this much. Your job is not to be their savior. It is to be their spouse, faithful and kind, and to trust the actual Savior with the part you were never strong enough to carry anyway.

To the spouse who is losing faith

You are not a villain, and you are probably being treated like one. Your doubt is likely honest, arrived at through real questions or real wounds, and you did not choose it to hurt anyone. Watching your spouse's pain is its own kind of agony. You feel guilty for something you cannot help, judged for being honest, and increasingly like a foreigner in a marriage that used to feel like home. I see you. Your integrity in not faking a faith you no longer feel is worth something, even if no one around you is saying so.

But I have to ask something of you too, because a marriage has two people and both bear responsibility for its care. Do not let your doubt become contempt. It is easy, when you have moved away from a belief, to start seeing your spouse's faith as foolish, to grow impatient with their grief, to treat their fear as irrational. That contempt will kill your marriage faster than the doubt ever could. The researcher John Gottman, who has studied thousands of married couples across decades at the University of Washington, identified contempt as the single strongest predictor of divorce, the acid that dissolves a marriage from within. Your spouse is not stupid for believing. They are grieving a real loss, the loss of the shared faith you both once had. Honor that grief the way you want them to honor your doubt. And do not, in your certainty that you have seen through the faith, become as dogmatic in your unbelief as you accuse them of being in their belief. Doubt held with humility is honest. Doubt held with contempt is just a new fundamentalism.

The marriage is not the theology

This is what can hold your marriage together while the faith question remains unresolved, and I say this as a pastor who has married and buried and counseled people for fifteen years. Your marriage is not primarily a shared set of beliefs. It is a covenant between two people. You did not marry a doctrinal statement. You married a person, and that person is still there, still the one you chose, still worthy of the vow you made. The vow said for better or for worse. Nobody puts this in their wedding vows, but this is the worse. This is exactly the kind of unforeseen weight the covenant was built to carry.

The temptation on both sides is to treat the faith difference as the whole marriage, to let it colonize every conversation and every interaction until you are no longer a husband and wife but two positions in an argument. Resist that. You are more than your beliefs about God, both of you. You still share children, a history, a home, a thousand ordinary acts of love. Do not let the one area of difference consume the many areas of union. Protect the marriage as a marriage while the faith question works itself out, and it may take years, and it may not resolve the way either of you wants. A marriage can hold two people who disagree about the largest thing, if they refuse to let the disagreement become their whole identity as a couple.

You married a person, not a doctrinal statement. The person is still there. The vow was built to carry exactly this weight. Do not set it down because the theology got hard.

I want to speak practically about the thing that will actually decide whether your marriage survives this, and it is not the theology. It is how you handle the daily friction the difference creates. Church on Sunday. What you tell the children. The prayer before dinner that one of you no longer means. The holidays. The friends who ask. These small collisions, if they are handled with contempt or ultimatums, will grind the marriage down long before any grand crisis of belief. If they are handled with negotiation and tenderness and a shared commitment to protect the union above winning the point, the marriage can absorb an astonishing amount of difference. Decide together, before the collisions come, that you will treat each other as allies working out a hard situation, not as opponents in a war of worldviews. The couples who survive this are not the ones who resolve the theology. They are the ones who refuse to let the theology make them enemies at the kitchen table.

Do not force the ending

To the believing spouse, do not conclude that a spouse who has lost faith is a spouse you are permitted or required to leave. Paul addressed this directly. "If any brother has a wife who is an unbeliever, and she consents to live with him, he should not divorce her. For the unbelieving husband is made holy because of his wife" (1 Corinthians 7:12 through 14). Your presence in the marriage is not compromised by your spouse's doubt. It may be the very thing God uses. And to the doubting spouse, do not conclude that because you have changed, the honest thing is to blow up the life you built. Honesty about your beliefs does not require dishonoring your covenant. You can be truthful about your doubt and faithful to your marriage at the same time. These are not in conflict, though the pressure will tempt you to treat them as if they are.

And to both of you, get help that honors both people. Find a counselor, ideally one who understands both the faith dimension and the marital dynamics, who will not simply take the side of belief or the side of doubt. This is not something most couples can carry alone, and reaching for help is not a sign the marriage is failing. It is a sign you are fighting for it. If the strain has grown so heavy that either of you is falling into a darkness that makes you not want to be here anymore, please reach out tonight. In the United States you can call or text 988. A marriage under this weight is worth protecting, and so is each of the two lives in it.

The verdict

One of you lost the faith you both once shared, and it has become a fault line running through your home. But a fault line is not a divorce, and a difference is not the end. The marriage you built was never only a shared theology. It was a covenant between two people who chose each other, and that covenant was designed to carry weights neither of you could foresee. This is one of them. It is heavy. It is not necessarily fatal.

Believing spouse, love your husband or wife without a word, so well that your faith is the most compelling thing in the house, and stop trying to win a debate you can only lose by fighting. Doubting spouse, hold your doubt with humility instead of contempt, and honor the grief of the person watching you change. Both of you, protect the marriage as a marriage while the question of God works itself out slowly, over years, in ways you cannot control. You do not have to agree about the largest thing to keep the vow you made. You only have to keep choosing the person you married, the one still sitting across the table, still worth the promise. The faith may return or it may not. The love does not have to leave with it. Guard that. It is the thing you can still choose today.
excerpt: You said your vows to two believers, and now there is only one. This is for the marriage where faith has quietly become a fault line.

title: Doubt and Aging: When Certainty Fades With the Body
body:
My oldest son asked me once whether faith gets easier as you get older. He was fifteen, and he assumed the doubts of youth were a phase you outgrow, like acne, like the fear of the dark. I told him the truth, which is that I did not know, because I was not old yet. I am closer now. And what I have watched in the older men I love has taught me something the youth version of this conversation never touches. The doubts that come with age are not the doubts of a college dorm. They do not arrive with fresh outrage or new arguments. They arrive with the body.

There is a particular kind of doubt that only shows up when the machinery starts to fail. When a man who prayed every morning of his life for forty years finds that the words feel like they are going into an empty room. When a woman who taught Sunday school for three decades watches her husband forget her name and wonders what all the theology was for. This is not the doubt of the skeptic who never believed. It is the doubt of the veteran who believed hard and long and is now being asked to believe through the failure of everything that once made belief feel warm.

The Body Was Always Part of the Argument

We do not admit how much of our faith runs on the body. The young Christian who feels God's presence in worship is, in part, feeling his own nervous system respond to music and community and the flood of chemistry that a healthy brain produces in a room full of people singing. I am not reducing the presence of God to neurochemistry. I am saying that the felt sense of that presence has always come to us through a body, and when the body stops cooperating, the felt sense goes quiet, and we mistake the silence of the instrument for the absence of the player.

The philosopher Charles Taylor, in his 2007 work A Secular Age, described what he called the buffered self, the modern person sealed off from a world once assumed to be full of spirits and meaning. But there is another buffering that happens later, and it is not cultural. It is physical. Age buffers you from the felt intensity of everything. The food tastes less. The music moves you less. And the presence of God, which came to you for years as a warmth in the chest, comes now as a memory of a warmth. This is not apostasy. It is aging. But it feels like abandonment, and no one warned you.

I say this as a man who came to faith from atheism, which means I remember the exact texture of unbelief. I know what the empty room feels like, because I lived in it for years before Christ found me. So when an older believer tells me that prayer feels like the empty room again, I do not panic, and I do not tell them to try harder. I tell them that the empty room is not proof of anything. It was not proof when I was a young atheist, and it is not proof now. The feeling of absence and the fact of absence are two different claims, and the whole tradition knew this long before neuroscience gave us the mechanism.

The Dark Night Was Never Only for Mystics

John of the Cross wrote The Dark Night of the Soul in the sixteenth century, sitting in a monastery cell after his own brothers imprisoned him. He described a stage in the life of faith where God withdraws the felt consolations that once carried the believer, not as punishment, but as maturation. The believer had been loving the gifts of God more than God. So the gifts are removed, and what remains is either a faith that loves God for himself, or the discovery that there was less faith there than anyone thought.

We have made this a boutique experience for spiritual athletes. It is not. It is the ordinary shape of a long life with God. The consolations that carried you at forty are meant to be removed at seventy, and the removal is not God leaving. It is God asking whether you loved him or loved how he made you feel. That is a brutal question to ask an eighty-year-old whose hands shake too much to hold the Bible they have read every day since 1962. But it is the question the whole tradition says love finally comes down to.

"My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever." (Psalm 73:26)

Read that verse again and notice what it does not say. It does not say the flesh might fail. It says the flesh will fail. The psalmist is not being brave about a hypothetical. He is looking directly at the certainty of his own decline and staking his claim on the far side of it. He does not deny that the heart fails. He denies that the failure of the heart is the last word about the heart. That is the sentence I want in front of every believer whose body is subtracting them one function at a time.

The Grief We Refuse to Name a Grief

There is a particular cruelty in how the church treats the doubt of the aging, and it is that we will not call it grief. We call it a lapse. We call it a season of dryness. We hand the eighty-year-old a devotional and tell them to press in, as though the problem were effort rather than loss. But what the aging believer is experiencing is a genuine bereavement, the loss of the felt companionship of God that carried them for decades, and grief cannot be argued away any more than the grief of a widow can be argued away. It has to be mourned.

The psychiatrist and writer Gerald May, in his 2004 book The Dark Night of the Soul, argued that much of what we medicate or scold as spiritual failure is actually the soul being led into a deeper and less feeling-dependent love. May, who spent decades working with people in crisis, insisted that the removal of consolation is often not the soul's disease but its healing, mistaken for disease because we have been trained to equate the presence of God with the feeling of his presence. When you have made that equation for sixty years, its breaking feels like death. But the equation was always false, and the breaking of a false thing, however painful, is a mercy.

I sit with the aging and I let them grieve. I do not rush them to the resolution. I let them say out loud that they miss the God they used to feel, that prayer used to be warm and now it is cold, that they are frightened by the silence. And then, only after the grief has been honored, I say the true thing, which is that the God they miss has not gone anywhere. He has only stopped giving them the feelings, and the feelings were never him. This is not a fix. It is a reframe that takes the pressure off the failing body to produce a warmth it can no longer manufacture. The warmth was never the point. The person behind the warmth was always the point, and he remains.

What My Own Father's Absence Taught Me About This

I was raised without a father, and one of the strange gifts of that wound is that I never had a human model of a man growing old with me. I did not watch a father age. So when I entered ministry and began sitting with dying men, I had no template, and I had to actually pay attention instead of reaching for a memory. What I learned is that the men who died well were not the men with the fewest doubts. They were the men who had made peace with holding faith and fear in the same hand.

There was a man in my congregation, a retired machinist, who told me in his last month that he was not sure of anything anymore. He had believed his whole life, and now the belief felt thin, and he was ashamed. I asked him what he still did, even without the certainty. He said he still prayed. He still said thank you before he ate, even when the food had no taste. He still asked God to take care of his wife. I told him that a man who keeps talking to God after the feeling is gone has more faith than the man who talks to God because it feels good. He did not believe me. He died anyway, still praying, and I will trust that God met the prayer and not the confidence behind it.

Certainty Was Never the Thing

Here is what age does to the whole project of certainty. It exposes it as a young person's category. When you are twenty, you want to be sure, because you have decades of life to arrange around the answer. When you are eighty, you have learned that you were sure of a hundred things that turned out to be wrong, and the ones you got right you often got right by accident. Certainty stops being the measure. What matters is whether you are facing the right direction when the light finally comes.

The theologian Lesslie Newbigin, writing in the 1980s after decades as a missionary in India, argued that certainty in the mathematical sense was never available to faith and never should have been the goal. Faith is not the elimination of doubt. It is commitment held in the presence of doubt, staked on a person rather than a proof. Newbigin called this proper confidence, and he was careful to distinguish it from certainty. Confidence can survive the failing of the body. Certainty was always going to break, because certainty depended on a mind that stays sharp, and no mind stays sharp forever.

This matters enormously for the aging believer, because so much of the fear is the fear that losing sharpness means losing salvation. It does not. The thief on the cross had no theology and one sentence of faith, and Christ told him he would be in paradise that day (Luke 23:43). A man with dementia who can no longer articulate the gospel is not thereby cut off from the God who articulated it to him. Grace does not require you to hold onto it with a strong grip. Grace holds you. That is the entire difference between the gospel and every religion of human effort, and it is exactly the difference the aging believer needs to hear.

When the Fear Is Real and Present

Some who read this are not describing a philosophy. They are describing a night that will not end, a fear that God has left, a body that hurts, and a mind that keeps circling the drain of despair. If that is you, hear this plainly. The feeling that God has abandoned you is not evidence that God has abandoned you. It is one of the oldest experiences in the faith, and the Psalms are full of it precisely so that you would know you are not the first. But feelings this heavy are not meant to be carried alone. Tell someone. Tell your pastor, tell your doctor, tell your children. There is help for the body and help for the mind, and asking for it is not a failure of faith. It is the faith doing exactly what it should, which is refusing to let you disappear into the dark quietly.

The despair says the story is over. It is lying. The story of a life with God does not end at the point of greatest weakness. That is precisely where the gospel says it turns. Christ did his most important work at his weakest, nailed and dying and apparently abandoned, crying out the opening line of Psalm 22 about being forsaken. If the Son of God went through the felt absence of the Father and came out the other side into resurrection, then your felt absence is not the exception to the faith. It is the pattern of the faith. You are walking where he walked.

The Verdict

The doubts of age are not a failure. They are the final examination of a faith that was always meant to outgrow its own scaffolding. The feelings were the scaffolding. The body was the scaffolding. Even the certainty was the scaffolding. What the tradition has always said, and what the dying men taught me when I had no father to teach me, is that under all of it there was a person, and the person does not age, and the person does not leave.

You will feel less. You will remember less. You may one day forget the words to the prayers you have said ten thousand times. But the God who found me in the empty room of atheism is the God who waits in the empty room of age, and he was never asking for your certainty. He was asking for your face turned toward him. Turn it there. The feeling is gone and the fact remains. Hold the fact.
excerpt: The doubts that come at sixty are not the doubts that came at twenty. They arrive quieter, and they cost more. Here is how faith survives the slow subtraction of the body.

title: The Youth Pastor Who Stopped Believing
body:
He came to my office on a Tuesday, which is the day pastors have their honest conversations, because Sunday is too raw and Monday is too tired. He was a youth pastor at a church across town, twenty-eight years old, and he told me that he did not believe anymore and he did not know how to stop performing that he did. He had a retreat in three weeks. He had forty teenagers who thought he was the most solid Christian they knew. And he had nothing left inside him but the muscle memory of belief.

I did not tell him what he expected me to tell him. He expected me to fix it, or to fire him in my heart, or to hand him a book of apologetics and send him home. What I told him was that he had just described the loneliest position in the church, and that I was not going to make it worse by pretending it was simple. The youth pastor who stops believing is not a rare defect. He is a common casualty of a system that asks young men to be spiritual professionals before they have been spiritual adults, and then acts shocked when the professional performance outlasts the belief that was supposed to fund it.

How the Faith Drained Out Without a Single Argument

Here is what surprised me most as he talked. There was no argument that broke him. He had not read the New Atheists and been convinced. He had not encountered a suffering he could not square with God. What had happened was slower and more corrosive than that. He had spent six years talking about God for a living, and somewhere in the talking, God had become a subject rather than a person. He had produced so many words about faith that he had used up his own.

The sociologist Christian Smith, in his 2005 study Soul Searching, coined a term for the actual religion of American teenagers. He called it moralistic therapeutic deism, a faith in a God who wants you to be nice, to feel good, and to stay largely out of your business until you need him. Smith's point that stung me was that the teenagers learned this faith from the adults. And the youth pastor is the front line of that transmission. He is handed a curriculum built to keep teenagers comfortable and mildly moral, and he is asked to be personally on fire for a God the curriculum has already reduced to a life coach. Of course the fire goes out. You cannot burn on fumes.

I asked him what he actually preached to the teenagers. He described talks about identity, about not comparing yourself to others, about God having a wonderful plan. I asked him when he had last preached the cross, the actual scandal of a God who died. He could not remember. He had been feeding teenagers spiritual snacks for years, and he had been living on the same snacks, and a man cannot survive on snacks. Neither can a faith. This was not primarily a crisis of belief. It was a crisis of malnourishment that had presented as a crisis of belief.

The Machine That Manufactures This Failure

I want to indict a system, and I want to indict myself as part of it, because I have hired youth pastors and handed them the same impossible assignment. The modern youth ministry model asks a young man in his twenties, often with no seminary training and little life experience, to be simultaneously an entertainer, a counselor, an event planner, a theologian, and a spiritual exemplar to thirty or forty teenagers who are watching him for signs that this whole thing is real. We pay him poorly, work him seventy hours a week, evaluate him by attendance numbers, and then we are surprised when the man cracks. We built the machine that broke him, and then we blame him for breaking.

The historian and pastor Eugene Peterson warned about this in his 1992 book Under the Unpredictable Plant, where he described how the pastoral vocation gets deformed into what he called religious careerism, the pastor turned into a manager of religious goods and services, measured by the growth of the enterprise rather than the depth of souls. Peterson saw that this deformation was spiritually lethal, because it required the pastor to perform a vitality he was too busy to actually possess. The youth pastor is the most exposed position in this whole system, because he works with the age group most sensitive to hypocrisy, and he must perform the most and is given the least to perform from. The wonder is not that some of them stop believing. The wonder is that any of them survive with a faith intact.

So when the man sat across from me, I did not see a spiritual failure. I saw a casualty of a machine that had used him up and would use up the next one just the same. And the first pastoral act was to tell him that, to lift the private shame off him and name the systemic thing that had ground him down. He had thought his emptiness was a moral failure, a sign that he was secretly a fraud. It was nothing of the kind. It was the predictable result of asking a man to give out water faster than anyone ever let him take any in.

The Difference Between Belief and Employment

The cruelest part of his situation was the entanglement of his faith with his paycheck. When an ordinary Christian doubts, they can sit in the back and say nothing and let the doubt run its course. When a youth pastor doubts, doubting means losing his income, his housing sometimes, his community entirely, and his identity as the person everyone counts on. So the pressure is enormous to fake it, and the faking accelerates the very death he is afraid of, because nothing kills faith faster than performing a faith you do not have.

"Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness." (James 3:1)

I read him that verse, and I told him it was not a threat. It was a mercy. James is warning that the position of the teacher is dangerous, that it carries a weight the ordinary believer does not carry. If James thought teaching was spiritually hazardous in the first century, how much more in a system that turns twenty-two-year-olds into spiritual authorities before they have suffered anything, before they have doubted anything, before they have had a faith tested enough to know whether it holds. The youth pastor who stops believing is not failing at an easy job. He is being crushed by a hard one that everyone pretends is easy.

What I Know About Standing on a Stage Empty

I came to faith from atheism, so I know the emptiness he described from the inside, but I know something else too. I have stood in a pulpit on a Sunday when I did not feel a thing, when the words came out of my mouth and I wondered if I meant them, when the congregation received a comfort I could not locate in myself. Every honest pastor has stood there. And the question that saved me, the question I gave him, was this. Is the truth of the gospel dependent on my current feeling of it, or is my feeling of it downstream of something that stays true whether I feel it or not.

Because if the gospel is true, it does not become false when I stop feeling it. The resurrection either happened in history around the year 30 or it did not, and my emotional state in 2026 does not vote on the matter. This is the great relief of a faith anchored in event rather than experience. My experience of the risen Christ can fail entirely, and the risen Christ is not thereby diminished. The scholar N.T. Wright spent seven hundred pages in his 2003 work The Resurrection of the Son of God making the historical case that something happened to the disciples that a hallucination cannot explain and a legend cannot account for. That case does not weaken when a youth pastor feels nothing. The object of faith and the feeling of faith are not the same object, and confusing them is what breaks men.

The Path That Is Not Deconstruction and Not Denial

He wanted to know his options, and he had reduced them to two. He could keep faking it, which was killing him, or he could blow up his life, quit, tell everyone, and start over as an unbeliever. I told him there was a third door, and it was the hardest and the only one worth walking through. He could stop faking, tell the truth to the right people, and let his faith be rebuilt from a foundation deeper than the youth ministry industrial complex had ever given him.

The first move was to tell the truth to someone with authority over him who would not fire him for honesty. This is the tragedy. Most youth pastors do not have such a person, because the system punishes exactly the honesty it most needs. So sometimes the right person is outside the employing church, a pastor across town, a counselor, a spiritual director who has walked men through this before. He needed to say the true sentence out loud to a safe person, because a doubt spoken to a trusted human loses half its terror, and a doubt kept secret grows in the dark until it swallows everything.

The second move was to stop producing words about God long enough to receive some. He needed a sabbatical from the stage, even a short one, because you cannot fill a bucket that is pouring out faster than you pour in. Eugene Peterson wrote in his 1987 book Working the Angles that the pastor's real work is prayer, Scripture, and spiritual direction, and that everything else is running the church rather than being a pastor. Peterson's warning was that pastors get so busy with the machinery of religion that they starve at the very well they are supposed to be tending. My friend had been running the machine for six years and had not drawn a bucket for himself in as long. No wonder he was dry.

Rebuilding on the Older Ground

The faith he had was not deep enough to lose. That sounds harsh. I mean it as hope. What drained out of him was a thin, therapeutic, experience-dependent Christianity that was never going to survive contact with real life. Its draining was not a tragedy. It was a clearing. Under the thin thing was the possibility of the older thing, the creedal faith the church has held for two thousand years, tested by persecution and plague and every argument the human mind has thrown at it. He had never actually stood on that ground. He had stood on the youth-camp version of it, and the youth-camp version cannot hold the weight of a grown man.

So I did not tell him to work up his old feelings. I told him to read the people who had faith under fire. Bonhoeffer writing from a Nazi prison. Augustine writing his Confessions in the fourth century about his own long unbelief and the God who chased him down. The Psalms, which contain more doubt per page than most sermons contain in a year. I told him to let the thin faith die and to see whether, in its death, he found himself standing on something that had been under it the whole time. That is not deconstruction, which takes the faith apart and stops. It is reconstruction, which digs down to the load-bearing ground and builds there.

A Word to the One Reading This on the Stage

If you are the youth pastor, or the worship leader, or the small-group host, and you have been performing a faith that left you months ago, hear this. You are not a fraud in the way you fear. A fraud never believed. You believed, and you are grieving, and grief and fraud are not the same sin. But you cannot keep performing, because the performance is the poison. It is time to tell someone the truth.

And if the emptiness has become something darker, if you have started to feel that the whole thing was a lie and that you would be better off gone, do not carry that in silence for one more night. That thought is not the truth telling you something. It is the exhaustion lying to you in the voice of clarity. Call someone tonight. A friend, a pastor, a counselor, a crisis line. The despair wants you alone, because it can only win in isolation. Deny it the isolation and you have already begun to deny it the victory.

The Verdict

The youth pastor who stopped believing did not lose the faith. He lost the counterfeit that had been standing in for it, and the loss felt like the end because he had never known there was anything underneath. There was. There always is. The God who found me in atheism is not smaller than the disappointment of a burned-out twenty-eight-year-old. He is not threatened by the honesty. He is waiting on the far side of it.

Get off the stage long enough to be found. Tell the truth to someone who will not punish you for it. And let the thin thing die so the real thing can come up under your feet. The retreat in three weeks is not more important than your soul. Cancel it if you have to. God can raise up someone to give the talk. He cannot easily raise up a man who spent his whole life performing a faith he never got to actually have.
excerpt: He led the retreats, wrote the talks, and prayed the prayers, and somewhere in the middle of it all the belief drained out of him. This is for the one still standing on the stage after the faith has gone.

title: When Your Entire Community Believes and You Don't
body:
There is a specific loneliness that has no name in most churches. It is the loneliness of the person who sits in the pew every week surrounded by people who seem entirely sure, singing songs about a certainty they no longer feel, shaking hands after the service and saying they are fine, and going home to a house where the doubt waits for them like an animal. The community believes. They do not. And they have learned that saying so out loud would cost them everyone they love.

I have sat with these people, and what strikes me every time is how alone they are in the middle of a crowd. It is one thing to doubt in a secular city where no one cares. It is another thing entirely to doubt inside a family, a small town, a church that is your entire social world, where your unbelief is not just your private problem but a threat to every relationship you have. That person is not weak. That person is carrying a weight most of the confident people around them have never had to lift.

The Sociology of Sacred Certainty

The sociologist Peter Berger described in his 1967 work The Sacred Canopy how communities construct what he called plausibility structures, the social scaffolding that makes a belief feel obvious and unquestionable. A belief held by everyone around you feels like a fact. A belief held by no one around you feels like madness, even if it is true. The point Berger made, which cuts both ways, is that certainty is often a social product rather than an intellectual one. The people in your church who seem so sure are, in part, sure because everyone around them is sure. Their certainty is being held up by the same social pressure that is crushing you.

This matters because it means your doubt is not necessarily a sign that you see less than they do. It may be a sign that you see more. You have stepped outside the plausibility structure enough to notice that it is a structure, and the vertigo you feel is the vertigo of standing where the ground is not being held up for you by the crowd. That is a terrifying place to stand. It is also, sometimes, the place where the most honest faith is finally forged, because a faith that survives outside the crowd's support is a faith you actually own rather than one you inherited.

I say this carefully, because I do not want to flatter your doubt into a badge of superiority. That is its own trap. The person who thinks their unbelief makes them smarter than the believers around them has simply traded one social pride for another. But I do want to break the equation that doubt equals defect. Sometimes the one person in the room who is not sure is the one person in the room who is taking God seriously enough to be honest about the difficulty.

The Faith the Crowd Never Tested

Consider what it means that the confident people around you have often never been tested the way you are being tested. A faith held up by a crowd has never had to stand on its own legs. It has never known whether it could survive the withdrawal of social approval, because the approval has never been withdrawn. This is not a criticism of those believers. It is simply an observation about the difference between a belief that has been load-tested and a belief that has not. Yours is being load-tested right now, in the worst possible conditions, and the fact that it hurts is not evidence that it is failing. It is evidence that it is being examined more rigorously than the comfortable faith around you has ever been.

The theologian Miroslav Volf, writing in his 1996 book Exclusion and Embrace out of the wreckage of the war in his native Croatia, observed that faith which has never been threatened has never had to become its own, that it remains borrowed until the moment it is contested. Volf was writing about faith under the pressure of ethnic hatred and violence, but the principle reaches your quieter situation. Until your faith is contested, it belongs to the crowd that gave it to you. When it is contested, and you either lose it or make it your own, it becomes for the first time genuinely yours. The doubter in the confident room is standing at the exact threshold where inherited faith either dies or becomes personal, and that threshold is a more honest place to stand than the comfortable middle of the crowd.

I do not say this to romanticize your pain. I say it to reframe what it means. You have assumed that your doubt places you below the confident believers, at the bottom of the spiritual hierarchy of the room. It may place you somewhere else entirely, at the one point in the room where faith is actually being decided rather than merely inherited. That is a lonely place. It is not a lesser place. Some of the deepest believers I have ever known passed through exactly this valley, and they came out with a faith that could no longer be taken from them, precisely because it had already survived being alone.

The Cost of the Mask

The mask is exhausting. You know this if you wear it. Every conversation is a small performance. Every prayer meeting is a rehearsal of words you no longer mean. Every time someone asks how your walk with God is going, you produce a sentence that keeps the peace and deepens the loneliness. And the deepest cruelty is this. The very community that could hold you, that exists in theory precisely to carry the ones who are struggling, is the community you cannot tell, because you have learned that struggling is not permitted here.

"Bear one another's burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ." (Galatians 6:2)

Read that verse and then look at your church and ask an honest question. Is this a community that bears burdens, or a community that hides them. Because a church where you cannot admit doubt is not bearing your burden. It is requiring you to hide it, which is the opposite of what Paul commands. That is not a failure on your part. It is a failure of the church's culture, and naming it as such is not bitterness. It is accuracy. A community that only accepts the certain has excluded most of the people the gospel was written for.

Why I Understand the Mask From Both Sides

I came to faith from atheism, which means for most of my life I was the unbeliever surrounded by believers who thought I was one of them or wished I would become one. I know the resentment of being handed certainties by people who had never doubted. And I was raised without a father, so I know the particular hunger of a person who wants to belong somewhere and fears that honesty will cost them the belonging. Those two experiences taught me not to trust a community that only has room for the confident, because I was never confident, and the communities that had no room for me were the ones I was right to keep my distance from.

But here is the turn. When Christ finally found me, he did not find me in a room full of certain people. He found me in my honesty, in the middle of my objections, in the place where I had stopped performing anything for anyone. The God of the Bible is not afraid of the doubter. He is afraid, if I can put it that way, of the liar, the one who has so mastered the performance of faith that they have deceived even themselves. Jesus was gentle with doubt and hard on hypocrisy. That should tell the doubter in the confident room exactly where they stand with God, whatever they stand with the crowd.

Finding the One Safe Person

You do not need to tell the whole community. That is a common mistake, to think the only alternative to hiding from everyone is confessing to everyone. You do not owe your doubt to the crowd. What you need, and what will actually begin to break the isolation, is one safe person. One. A single human being who can hear the true sentence and not flinch, not fix, not report you to the elders, not treat you as a project. One person changes everything, because the doubt that is spoken to one trusted human loses its power to define you in secret.

Finding that person takes discernment, and sometimes they are not inside your immediate community. Sometimes the safe person is a pastor from another church, a counselor, a friend who left the faith and can hold your doubt without either celebrating it or panicking at it. The theologian Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing his 1938 book Life Together about a community that would soon be scattered by the Gestapo, argued that the Christian who cannot be alone should beware of community, and the Christian who cannot be in community should beware of being alone. You need both. You need the solitude to be honest with God without an audience, and you need the one person who proves that honesty does not equal exile.

When Leaving Feels Like the Only Air

Some who read this have concluded that the only way to be honest is to leave, to walk away from the community entirely, because staying means lying and lying is unbearable. I understand the logic, and I will not tell you it is always wrong. Sometimes a community is so hostile to honesty that staying really would require the death of your integrity, and no faith is worth that price. But I will offer one caution, learned from watching many people walk this road.

The people who leave in a burst of relief often discover, a year later, that they traded one loneliness for another. They escaped the loneliness of hiding among believers and inherited the loneliness of having no one who shares the deepest questions of their life. The doubt did not resolve by leaving. It just lost the last people who might have walked with it. So before you leave, ask whether the problem is the faith or the community's handling of it, because those are different problems, and leaving solves at most one of them. Sometimes the answer is a different church, not no church. Sometimes it is finding the honest remnant inside the church you have. Leaving should be a considered decision, not an escape from a room you were never given permission to be honest in.

I say this as a man who spent years outside every believing community and knows exactly what that costs. Being raised without a father, I learned early to be the person on the edge of every room, watching, never fully belonging, and I carried that into my years as an atheist, where I told myself the distance was freedom. It was not freedom. It was exile with a better name. When people describe the relief of walking away from a church that suffocated their honesty, I believe them, and I also know what waits on the other side, because I lived there, and the loneliness of the empty room is not less than the loneliness of the crowded one. It is only quieter, and quiet loneliness is easier to mistake for peace.

So I do not tell people never to leave. I tell them to count the cost honestly, both costs, the cost of staying dishonest and the cost of leaving lonely, and to make sure that whatever they choose, they do not do it alone and do not do it in a single wounded night. The decision to leave a community is one of the most significant a person makes, and it deserves to be made in daylight, with counsel, over time, and not as a reflex against a room that hurt. Wounds heal badly when the treatment is only escape.

The Weight I Will Not Lift Off You

If your doubt has curdled into something heavier, if the isolation has convinced you that you are fundamentally alone in the universe and that the aloneness is unbearable, please hear this before you read another word. That feeling is real and it is also lying to you about its permanence. You are not the only one, even if you are the only one in your particular pew. And the weight you are carrying is not a weight you were built to carry by yourself. If the darkness has started to whisper that everyone would be better off without you, that is the exhaustion talking, not the truth, and it is time to tell someone tonight. A crisis line, a doctor, a friend, anyone with a pulse who will stay on the phone. You do not have to solve the theology first. You just have to not be alone with the dark right now.

The despair is a liar with a very specific lie, which is that no one could understand and no one would stay. I have watched that lie proven false a hundred times. The moment the true sentence leaves your mouth to a safe person, the lie loses its footing, because it turns out someone can hear it and stay. Give someone that chance. Deny the isolation the silence it feeds on.

The Verdict

Being the only doubter in a room full of the certain is one of the loneliest positions in the Christian life, and the loneliness is not a punishment for your unbelief. It is a symptom of a community that has made no room for the very struggle the gospel was built to hold. You are not less faithful than the confident crowd. You may simply be more honest, and honesty in a dishonest room always feels like isolation.

Find the one safe person. Keep the solitude that lets you be honest with God without an audience. And do not mistake the community's failure to hold your doubt for God's refusal to hold it. The God who found me outside every certain room is not waiting for you inside the crowd's certainty. He is waiting in your honesty, which is the one place the crowd never taught you he could be. Go there. He is already there, and he is not alone in the way you have been.
excerpt: You are surrounded by people who are sure, and you are the only one in the room who isn't. The isolation of hidden doubt is its own kind of suffering. Here is how to survive the room without lying in it.

title: Doubt as a Spiritual Practice
body:
We have been taught to treat doubt like an infection, something to be quarantined, cured, and never spoken of again. Get the doubt out of you, the thinking goes, and get back to the healthy state of certainty as fast as possible. I want to argue something the church has half-forgotten, which is that doubt handled rightly is not an infection at all. It is a discipline. It is a practice that can be entered on purpose, worked through with intention, and used to build a faith stronger than the one that never questioned anything.

This is dangerous ground and I know it. There is a kind of doubt that corrodes, and I am not going to pretend it does not exist. But there is another kind, an older and more honorable kind, that the great believers have always practiced deliberately, and treating all doubt as the corroding kind has left the church defenseless against the very questions that could have deepened it. I came to faith from atheism, so I know both kinds intimately. And I have come to believe that the church's fear of doubt has done more damage than doubt itself ever did.

The Tradition Doubted on Purpose

Start with the Psalms, because they are the prayer book Jesus himself prayed. Roughly a third of them are laments, and many of those laments are not gentle. Psalm 88 ends in darkness with no resolution. The psalmist accuses God of hiding, of casting him off, of surrounding him with terrors, and the psalm simply stops there, in the dark. Whoever assembled the Psalter did not edit that one out to keep the tone positive. They left it in the middle of Scripture, a permanent permission slip for the believer who prays into a silence.

"O Lord, why do you cast my soul away? Why do you hide your face from me?" (Psalm 88:14)

That is a doubt spoken directly to God, and God preserved it in his own book. Think about what that means. The God who could have given us only the confident psalms chose to give us the doubting ones too, which tells you that he considers the honest question a form of worship rather than a betrayal of it. The medieval theologians had a phrase, fides quaerens intellectum, faith seeking understanding, which Anselm used in the eleventh century as the subtitle of his Proslogion. Faith was not the end of questioning. It was the thing that made the questioning possible, because you can only question honestly when you trust that the answer will not destroy you.

The Difference Between the Two Doubts

Everything turns on a distinction the church usually collapses. There is a doubt that is looking for an exit, and there is a doubt that is looking for the truth. They can feel identical from the inside, but they move in opposite directions. The doubt looking for an exit gathers objections and refuses answers, because the answers threaten the exit it wants. The doubt looking for truth gathers objections and actually weighs the answers, willing to be persuaded either way, because it wants what is real more than it wants any particular outcome.

The philosopher and mathematician Blaise Pascal understood this in the seventeenth century. In the Pensees, published after his death in 1662, he distinguished between those who seek God and have not found him and those who neither seek nor find. Of the seekers he said they were miserable and reasonable. Of the non-seekers he said they were miserable and unreasonable. The point is that seeking doubt, doubt that is actually looking, is a reasonable and honorable state, even when it has not yet arrived. God is not offended by the seeker. He is grieved by the one who has stopped looking and calls the stopping wisdom.

So the first discipline of doubt as a practice is to interrogate your own doubt and ask which kind it is. Are you looking for the truth, or are you looking for permission to leave. If you are looking for permission to leave, no answer will satisfy you, because you have already decided. But if you are looking for the truth, then your doubt is not the enemy of faith. It is faith's advance scout, sent ahead into the hard country to find out whether the ground will hold.

How to Doubt on Purpose

Doubt as a practice means bringing the questions into the light on a schedule rather than letting them ambush you at three in the morning. I tell people to actually write down the doubt in its strongest form, the version their most intelligent unbelieving friend would recognize, not a straw version they can easily knock down. Writing it strong is an act of respect for the truth. If your faith can only survive the weak version of the objection, it cannot survive, and better to know that now.

Then, having stated the doubt at its strongest, you go looking for the strongest answer, not the first answer, not the pat answer from a youth group, but the answer that has satisfied serious minds. This is why the practice requires reading. The theologian C.S. Lewis, who like me came to faith from atheism, wrote in his 1955 memoir Surprised by Joy about how his own unbelief was slowly dismantled not by a single argument but by an honest and sustained looking, a refusal to settle for either easy faith or easy denial. Lewis called himself, in the year of his conversion, the most reluctant convert in all England. His faith was strong precisely because it had been forced through doubt rather than around it.

The practice also means sitting with the questions that do not resolve, and this is the part most people skip. Some doubts do not get answered in this life. The problem of a child's suffering does not resolve into a tidy theodicy that makes the suffering fine. The discipline is not to force a resolution that is not there but to hold the unresolved question inside the faith rather than letting it drive you out. You can believe firmly in a God whose ways you do not fully understand. In fact you must, because a God you fully understood would be a God small enough to fit inside your head, which is to say an idol.

The Wound That Taught Me to Doubt Well

I was raised without a father, and one of the things that absence teaches you is that some questions do not get answered by anyone showing up to answer them. As a boy I asked where he was and why he left, and the questions hung in the air unanswered for years. That could have made me a person who demands an answer before he will trust anything. Instead, strangely, it made me a person who learned to live with an open question without letting the openness eat me. When I came to faith, that skill transferred. I did not need God to answer every question before I would trust him. I had already learned, the hard way, that you can love and trust in the presence of a question that will not close.

This is what I mean by doubt as a practice. It is the muscle of holding faith and question in the same hand, and that muscle is built by exercise. Every time you bring a doubt into the light, examine it honestly, weigh the strongest answer, and then keep trusting God whether or not the doubt fully resolved, you have strengthened the muscle. The believer who has never doubted has a faith like an untested bridge. It may hold. But no one knows, least of all them, and the first real weight may bring it down. The believer who has doubted on purpose and kept believing has a bridge that has been load-tested, and they know what it can carry.

There is a further gift in this that the certain never receive. The believer who has practiced doubt becomes safe for other doubters. He does not flinch when someone confesses that they are not sure, because he has been not sure, on purpose, in daylight, and lived. The certain believer, however sincere, often cannot help the doubter, because he has never been where the doubter is and treats the doubt as an alien thing to be feared or fixed. The one who has practiced doubt can sit in it with another person, unhurried, unafraid, because he knows the ground on the far side of it. In this way the discipline of your own doubt becomes an instrument of care for someone else's, and the very thing you were ashamed of becomes the thing that lets you meet another person in the dark and not leave them there alone. Few gifts in the church are rarer than a believer who is not frightened of a question.

The Company of the Doubting Faithful

One reason doubt feels like exile is that we imagine the great believers as men and women of untroubled certainty, and so our own trouble feels like disqualification. The history says otherwise. Mother Teresa, whose private letters were published in 2007 as Come Be My Light, spent nearly fifty years in what she described as a spiritual darkness so profound that she often could not feel God at all, and she served the dying of Calcutta the entire time. She doubted the felt presence of God for decades and gave her whole life to Christ anyway. If that is not faith, the word has no meaning. Her doubt did not disqualify her service. It was the very soil her service grew in.

The point is not that doubt is comfortable. Teresa's letters are agonized. The point is that doubt and deep, world-changing faithfulness have coexisted in the same soul across the whole history of the church, and the person who treats their own doubt as proof of their unfitness has simply never been told the truth about the people they most admire. Thomas doubted and became an apostle. The father in Mark 9 doubted and his son was healed. Teresa doubted and fed the dying for half a century. You are in company you did not know you had, and the company is not the company of the failed. It is the company of the faithful, who happened to be honest about the cost.

This is why the practice of doubt, done rightly, ends not in isolation but in solidarity. When you stop treating your doubt as a private shame and start seeing it as a shared feature of the deepest faith, the whole thing changes. You are no longer the one broken believer in a church of the certain.
